title: Minimum recommended distances between cardiac implantable electronic devices and the applicator surface in low-energy intraoperative radiotherapy of the breast: an in vivo dosimetric study.
abstract: Purpose Clinical guidelines recommend keeping the dose to cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) below 2 Gy. In low-energy intraoperative radiotherapy (IORT) of the breast, the Intrabeam treatment planning system (TPS) estimates dose in water, without accounting for tissue attenuation, reduced scatter at the skin surface and backscatter from tungsten shielding. This study aimed to determine conservative minimum recommended distances between the CIED and the applicator surface based on in vivo dosimetry. Materials and methods Thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLDs), cross-calibrated against an ionization chamber, were placed on the skin between the applicator and the infraclavicular region, close to the usual CIED location, in 21 patients undergoing breast IORT. Applicator-to-dosimeter distances were measured with intraoperative ultrasound, and dose-distance curves were fitted to identify the distance at which dose falls below 2 Gy (d <2Gy ). Results Tungsten shielding increased the surface dose by approximately 22%, whereas without shielding the surface dose in water was on average 3% lower than predicted under full-scatter conditions. The median d <2Gy exceeded the TPS value by 3.1 mm (interquartile range -1.7 to 4.5 mm), with large inter-patient variability. Minimum recommended distances, defined as the upper 95% confidence limit of the regression of d <2Gy on applicator diameter, ranged from 29 mm (35 mm applicator) to 39 mm (50 mm applicator), compared with 22-24 mm calculated by the TPS. Conclusion Intraoperative ultrasound combined with applicator-specific minimum recommended distances provides a practical tool to guide treatment decisions in patients with CIEDs undergoing low-energy breast IORT.

title: PROton therapy for HPV-related oroPHaryngeal cancer patients using normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) modEl-based strategy: an iTalian multIcenter retrospective Cross-sectional study - PROPHETIC.
abstract: Background Intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) has shown promise in reducing toxicityfor patients with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC), while maintaining comparable tumor control to intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT). However, technical, logistical and economic factors have limited widespread implementation. Methods We conducted the first Italian multicenter in-silico comparative study of photon and proton plans in 100 patients with HPV-related OPSCC, involving seven radiation oncology departments. Clinical photon-based plans (mostly using Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT)) were compared with robustly optimized IMPT plans generated using the CNAO beamline. Dosimetric endpoints and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) values for xerostomia and dysphagia were assessed. Eligibility for IMPT was retrospectively estimated using the Dutch model-based selection (MBS)criteria. Results Target coverage was comparable between modalities, although IMPT plans showed slightly lower conformity indices. IMPT significantly reduced the dose bath to healthy tissues, with lower mean doses to the parotids, submandibular glands, pharyngeal constrictors, oral cavity, brainstem, and spinal cord (p < 0.01). NTCP analyses predicted clinically relevant reductions in xerostomia and dysphagia with IMPT. Applying the MBS approach, 36 % of patients were deemed eligible for PT, consistent with previous reports. Inter-center variability in eligibility reflected differences in delineation practices and clinical protocols. Conclusions This study tested the feasibility of a multicenter model-based evaluation for IMPT in Italy. A substantial proportion of OPSCC patients could benefit from IMPT, though results likely represent a conservative estimate due to protocol choices. Standardized delineation, robust optimization, and integration of NTCP models are essential for consistent patient selection.

title: Single prior-based 3D volumetric tracking from a planar snapshot in spine SBRT: A proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Background Continuous 3D onboard monitoring is essential to ensure accurate dose delivery of stereotactic body radiation therapy. However, current approaches for 2D-to-3D volumetric estimation typically require extensive patient-specific data, or depend on auxiliary imaging hardware. This study introduces a proof-of-concept framework for data-efficient, patient-specific 3D volumetric tracking using only a single volumetric prior. Methods A retrospective dataset of 80 spine SBRT patients was utilized. Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs synthesized from cone-beam computed tomography volumes served as surrogates for onboard kV projections. The pipeline consists of patient-agnostic pre-training using an archival dataset, patient-specific adaptation using the single volumetric prior supplemented by non-rigid motion simulations, and simulated intra-fractional 3D estimation. The network employs a modified Attention U-Net with a channel-to-depth bottleneck and a triple feature concatenation to map the 2D to 3D spatial domain. Results The proposed model demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in structural tracking capabilities compared to a static uncompensated baseline. Furthermore, the performance variance across patients was substantially compressed, enhancing reliability against setup uncertainties while achieving high spatial concordance in the complex spinal anatomy. The inference throughput reached approximately 10 frames per second. Conclusions This proof-of-concept study establishes the technical feasibility of data-efficient, patient-specific onboard volumetric tracking using a single volumetric prior by successfully resolving anatomical deformations from a single 2D projection in near real-time.

title: Efficient proton adaptive breast radiotherapy with CBCT-Based synthetic CT.
abstract: Purpose Repeat CTs (reCTs) are routinely used during breast proton radiotherapy to assess anatomical and positioning changes; however, they increase patient dose and workflow burden. This study evaluated CBCT-based synthetic CT imaging for accurately monitoring fractional dose distribution and developed an adaptive workflow for breast proton therapy. Methods A retrospective analysis included 26 breast cancer patients who received both CBCT and reCT on the same day between 2022 and 2024. Two commercial synthetic CT algorithms were studied: corrected CBCT (corrCBCT), which utilizes iterative correction, and virtual CT (vCT), generated by deforming the planning CT to match the CBCT. Treatment plans were recalculated on the corrCBCT and vCT, and compared with same-day reCT metrics. A prospective evaluation of weekly vCT-guided dosimetry was performed in an additional 25 patients to assess its feasibility in adaptive workflows. Results CorrCBCT and vCT produced reliable dosimetric results when compared with reCT. Target coverage, measured by the mean percentage dose difference in D95% to the breast or chest wall, was -0.80% (SD = 1.3) for the corrCBCT and -0.7% (SD = 1.6) for the vCT. vCT also showed good agreement with same-day reCT imaging for dose metrics of adjacent critical structures. Larger discrepancies were observed in nodal targets, primarily due to CBCT image artifacts in the shoulder region. Conclusion Accurate proton-dose calculations require reCT, but synthetic CT can effectively flag tissue alterations. This study shows that monitoring dosimetric shifts from vCT can prompt targeted reCT-based replanning in unilateral breast proton therapy, thereby sparing patients the exposure and logistics of routine reCT during treatment.

title: CT-ED/MD calibration curve commissioning and end-to-end validation of HyperSight CBCT-Based dose calculation for online adaptive radiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose To establish a CT number-to-electron/mass density (CT-ED/MD) calibration curve for the HyperSight cone-beam CT (CBCT) system on the Ethos platform, perform end-to-end dosimetric validation, and evaluate whether a single curve applies across kV imaging energies. Methods An electron density phantom (CIRS 062 M) was scanned at 125 and 140 kV and reconstructed using iterative CBCT (iCBCT) Acuros and metal artifact reduction (MAR) algorithms. A 125-kV curve was generated from the averaged Acuros/MAR HU values. Ten intensity-modulated radiotherapy/volumetric-modulated arc therapy plans spanning five disease sites (glioma, brain stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT), mediastinal tumor, lung stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), and prostate cancer) were created on simulation CT for anthropomorphic head, thorax, and pelvis phantoms and recalculated on HyperSight images using the single curve. Validation included ionization-chamber point-dose measurement, 3D gamma analysis, dose-volume histogram comparison, and equivalence testing. Results The averaged 125-kV curve agreed closely with the Philips 120-kV simulation CT curve. All 50 point-dose comparisons fell within ± 2% (82% within ± 1%), with mean differences of -0.24% to + 0.03% across disease sites, kV energies, and reconstruction algorithms. Mean body gamma pass rates were 99.79% (1%/1 mm) and 99.97% (2%/2 mm); mean target pass rates were 98.04% and 99.79%. Target mean-dose differences versus simulation CT averaged 0.11% (maximum 0.46%), and equivalence was confirmed within ± 2%. Conclusions A single, locally generated 125-kV CT-ED/MD curve based on averaged Acuros/MAR HU values enables clinically acceptable HyperSight-based dose calculation, supporting a simplified single-curve commissioning workflow for online adaptive radiotherapy.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI for Parkinson Disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Introduction Objective: The diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains challenging due to clinical overlap with other parkinsonian syndromes and the absence of widely available imaging biomarkers. Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) enables in vivo visualization of neuromelanin in the substantia nigra (SN) and locus coeruleus (LC), where signal loss reflects dopaminergic neurodegeneration in the SN and noradrenergic neurodegeneration in the LC. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in differentiating PD from healthy controls. Materials and methods PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to February 2025. Studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in PD versus healthy controls were included. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed methodological quality using QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated using a random-effects bivariate model, with construction of a summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve. Subgroup analyses were performed by anatomical region (SN, LC) and imaging parameter (volume, area, signal intensity, contrast ratio, subjective assessment), along with meta-regression and Deeks' funnel plot for publication bias. This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251088071). Results Twenty-eight studies comprising 2,268 participants were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were 88.0 % (95 % CI, 85.3-90.2 %) and 84.4 % (95 % CI, 80.6-87.5 %), respectively, with an area under the SROC curve of 0.901 and low heterogeneity (I 2 = 3.6 % for sensitivity, 9.2 % for specificity). Volumetric analysis of the SN yielded robust and reproducible performance (sensitivity 88.0 %, specificity 85.5 %), while subjective visual assessment achieved the highest sensitivity (90.8 %) but lower reproducibility. Meta-regression identified no significant effect of MRI acquisition parameters on diagnostic accuracy, and no significant publication bias was detected. Conclusion NM-MRI demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy for differentiating PD from healthy controls, with volumetric analysis of the substantia nigra offering a robust and reproducible imaging biomarker. As the included studies compared PD with healthy controls rather than with other parkinsonian syndromes, these findings should not yet be extrapolated to the differential diagnosis of PD from other forms of parkinsonism.

This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in differentiating PD from healthy controls.

PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to February 2025. Studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in PD versus healthy controls were included. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed methodological quality using QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated using a random-effects bivariate model, with construction of a summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve. Subgroup analyses were performed by anatomical region (SN, LC) and imaging parameter (volume, area, signal intensity, contrast ratio, subjective assessment), along with meta-regression and Deeks' funnel plot for publication bias. This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251088071).

Results

Twenty-eight studies comprising 2,268 participants were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were 88.0 % (95 % CI, 85.3-90.2 %) and 84.4 % (95 % CI, 80.6-87.5 %), respectively, with an area under the SROC curve of 0.901 and low heterogeneity (I2 = 3.6 % for sensitivity, 9.2 % for specificity). Volumetric analysis of the SN yielded robust and reproducible performance (sensitivity 88.0 %, specificity 85.5 %), while subjective visual assessment achieved the highest sensitivity (90.8 %) but lower reproducibility. Meta-regression identified no significant effect of MRI acquisition parameters on diagnostic accuracy, and no significant publication bias was detected.

Conclusion

NM-MRI demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy for differentiating PD from healthy controls, with volumetric analysis of the substantia nigra offering a robust and reproducible imaging biomarker. As the included studies compared PD with healthy controls rather than with other parkinsonian syndromes, these findings should not yet be extrapolated to the differential diagnosis of PD from other forms of parkinsonism.

title: Upper airway morphometry in acute neck infections: Clinical associations and deep learning-based segmentation.
abstract: Objectives Upper airway (UA) compromise is a significant and potentially life-threatening complication of acute neck infection (ANI), but objective, quantitative imaging features are lacking. This study aimed to evaluate the association between UA morphometry in emergency neck MRI and disease severity in ANI, and to develop and evaluate a deep learning (DL)-based model for automatic UA segmentation in ANI patients. Materials and methods A total of 322 patients were included. UA lumen was manually segmented, and prespecified morphometric features were extracted. UA morphometry was correlated with clinical outcomes. Interobserver agreement for all extracted features was evaluated with the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). An nnU-Net model was trained on manually segmented data, and its performance was evaluated using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and feature-specific ICCs. Results ICU admission occurred in 33/322 patients (10.2 %) and prolonged stay (>5 days) in 47/319 (14.7 %). Minimum cross-sectional area, compactness, maximum midline shift, and length of airway narrowing were associated with ICU admission (false-discovery-rate q ≤ 0.008) but not with prolonged stay, and did not significantly improve an established clinical model (AUC 0.80 to 0.84, DeLong p = 0.07 to 0.12). Interobserver agreement was moderate-to-excellent. The nnU-Net reached a median DSC of 0.920 with ICCs of 0.853 to 0.973 and reproduced the ICU associations. Conclusion Quantitative UA morphometry in ANI is reproducible. A narrow caliber, a long narrowed segment, and lateral displacement of the airway are associated with ICU admission, without demonstrated incremental value over established predictors in the prespecified comparison. nnU-Net segmentation reproduces the features and their univariable associations.

title: Prognostic value of native T1 mapping and extracellular volume fraction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Accurate risk stratification in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) remains challenging, and the prognostic significance of cardiovascular magnetic resonance-derived native T1 mapping and extracellular volume fraction (ECV) remains uncertain. Aims To systematically evaluate the prognostic value of native T1 mapping and ECV in HCM patients. Methods PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to February 6, 2026. Eligible studies assessed native T1 and/or ECV for prognosis in HCM. Baseline values, mean differences, and hazard ratios (HRs) were synthesized using random-effects models. Effect estimates were standardized as HRs per 30-ms increase in native T1 and per 1% increase in ECV. Results Eight longitudinal cohort studies involving 2539 HCM patients were included. Elevated native T1 was significantly associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (HR=1.27, 95% CI: 1.12-1.44, P < 0.001), as was higher ECV (HR=1.10, 95% CI: 1.07-1.14, P < 0.001). For sudden cardiac death-related outcomes, the association with native T1 was not significant, whereas elevated ECV was associated with an increased risk (HR=1.14, 95% CI: 1.01-1.28, P = 0.04), although substantial heterogeneity was observed and sensitivity analysis indicated limited robustness (HR=1.05, 95% CI: 0.97-1.14, P = 0.21). For heart failure-related outcomes, only ECV was associated with risk (HR=1.10, 95% CI: 1.05-1.15; P < 0.001). Conclusions Native T1 and ECV were associated with MACE risk in HCM, and ECV was additionally associated with heart failure-related outcomes. Their value for sudden cardiac death-related risk prediction requires further validation. Prospero registration number CRD420261406609.

title: Prognosis of Patients with Delayed Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Rupture after Endovascular Aortic Repair: A Multicentre Retrospective Study in France.
abstract: Objective The majority of patients with abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) undergo endovascular aortic repair (EVAR). Despite its high overall success rate, EVAR does not eliminate the risk of aneurysm rupture. This study aimed to evaluate the prognosis of patients undergoing surgical management for post-EVAR rupture. Methods A multicentre retrospective study of patients who presented with ruptured AAA after successful EVAR between 2007 and 2022 at 22 academic hospitals was conducted. The index EVAR procedures were performed between 2002 and 2020. Data were extracted from electronic hospital records and computed tomography scans. Death during follow up was ascertained using the French register of deceased persons. Survival probabilities at 30, 90, and 365 days were estimated with Kaplan-Meier estimators. Cox proportional hazards survival regression was used to identify determinants associated with increased risk of death. Results One hundred and nine patients (96 men) were included, with a mean age of 79.1 ± 9 years at the time of rupture. The median time from index EVAR to rupture was 50 months (range 0 - 179 months). Sixty-seven patients had open surgery (of which 37% underwent suprarenal cross clamping), 39 received endovascular treatment, and three underwent hybrid repair. Overall mortality was 26.6% at thirty days, increasing to 33.9% at ninety days, and 41.3% at 1 year. Neither the type of endoleak nor the type of repair was significantly associated with risk of death during follow up. Post-operative complications were frequent, including renal complications (44.0%), major haemorrhage (22.9%), respiratory distress (19.3%), and mesenteric ischaemia (6%). Conclusion This study presented a large multicentre series of patients treated for ruptured AAA after EVAR. Despite considerable progress in stent graft technology, EVAR offers little protection in the event of late rupture, even among patients with type II endoleak only. The mortality rate in this study is within the range of those published based on de novo AAA rupture.

title: Morphometric MRI analysis of the isthmus tonsillaris in patients with crossbite.
abstract: Background To characterize the minimum cross-sectional area of the isthmus tonsillaris using standardized magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and investigate its association with crossbite. Methods This retrospective observational study included standardized MRI examinations performed between 2002 and 2008. Thirty-six untreated subjects fulfilled the predefined inclusion criteria, comprising 26 patients with anterior and/or posterior crossbite and 10 controls with normal transverse occlusion. The minimum cross-sectional area of the isthmus tonsillaris was measured using a standardized morphometric MRI protocol. Group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Exploratory analyses investigated associations with age and transverse discrepancy. Results The mean minimum cross-sectional area measured 42.29 mm² in the crossbite group and 139.9 mm² in controls. No overlap was observed: the highest value in the crossbite group (80.5 mm²) remained below the lowest value in controls (87.0 mm²) (P < 0.001). No relevant differences were identified between sexes or crossbite subtypes. No linear association was found between negative transverse discrepancy and the minimum cross-sectional area. Exploratory analysis suggested an age-related increase in the minimum cross-sectional area in subjects with normal transverse occlusion, whereas this developmental pattern was not observed in patients with crossbite. Conclusions Patients with anterior and/or posterior crossbite demonstrated a reduced minimum cross-sectional area of the isthmus tonsillaris compared with subjects with normal transverse occlusion. These findings identify the isthmus tonsillaris as a relevant anatomical region warranting investigation in orthodontic diagnosis and interdisciplinary airway research. Future cone-beam computed tomography studies may provide datasets to validate these findings while adhering to the ALARA principle.

title: Impact of BRCA2, BRCA1, and Other Individual Homologous Recombination Repair Alterations on Survival in Metastatic Castration-resistant Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Background and objective The clinical significance of homologous recombination repair (HRR) alterations beyond BRCA2 in advanced prostate cancer is poorly understood. We investigated the association of individual non-BRCA2 HRR alterations with outcomes of patients treated with first-line therapy for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. Methods Eligible patients from the prospective CAPTURE study underwent somatic/germ line DNA analyses using a next-generation sequencing panel including ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, BRIP1, CDK12, CHEK2, FANCA, HDAC2, PALB2, RAD51B, and RAD54L. Association with overall survival (OS) and radiographic progression-free survival was assessed using multivariable Cox regression models comparing individual non-BRCA2 HRR alterations to those in patients with BRCA2 alterations or without HRR alterations. Key findings and limitations A total of 1010 patients were included, with BRCA2 and non-BRCA2 HRR alterations found in 122 (12%) and 191 (19%) patients, respectively. BRCA1, ATM, FANCA, HDAC2, CHEK2, CDK12, and BRIP1 alterations were observed in 19 (1.9%), 69 (6.8%), 34 (3.4%), 24 (2.4%), 23 (2.3%), 20 (2%), and 15 (1.5%) patients, respectively. Patients with ATM (hazard ratio [HR] 1.66; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.20-2.30; p = 0.002) or CHEK2 (HR 1.71; 95% CI = 1.03-2.90; p = 0.039) alterations showed improved OS compared to patients with BRCA2 alterations, with similar outcomes to patients without HRR alterations. BRCA1 (HR 0.49; 95% CI = 0.30-0.80; p = 0.004), FANCA (HR 0.61; 95% CI = 0.42-0.89; p = 0.011), and CDK12 (HR 0.57; 95% CI = 0.35-0.93; p = 0.025) were associated with worse OS compared to patients without HRR alterations, with similar outcomes to patients with BRCA2 alterations. Conclusions and clinical implications Prognostic associations differ across individual HRR alterations. Although BRCA1, FANCA, or HDAC mutations were associated with a prognosis similar to that associated with BRCA2 alterations, prognosis in patients with ATM or CHEK2 alterations was similar to that in patients without HRR alterations. In the research setting, non-BRCA2 HRR alterations should be analyzed and reported as individual entities whenever possible.

title: An OCT-based Structural Evaluation Framework for Laser-Induced Retinal Lesions in Mice and Exploratory Application Under ALDH2 Modulation.
abstract: Laser-induced retinal injury models require structural assessments that capture lesion heterogeneity. We developed a five-dimensional optical coherence tomography (OCT) framework and explored its application under aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) modulation. Following 532-nm left-eye photocoagulation, mice received dimethyl sulfoxide vehicle, Alda-1, or Daidzin intraperitoneally for seven days. OCT, fundus photography, and fluorescein angiography were performed 24 h after the final dose. The framework integrated morphologic classification, five-domain severity scoring, lesion geometry, layer-specific thickness and normalized area under the thickness-distance curve (AUC), and anatomically matched contralateral comparisons. Thirty-six lesions from nine mice were analyzed. Classification and scoring showed high interobserver agreement (κ = 0.839; intraclass correlation coefficient = 0.925). After Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, severity score was the only tested outcome differing significantly among subtypes; eight of 45 structural correlations were significant. In 32 matched pairs, all six thickness comparisons showed significantly lower lesion-eye values. Correlations between local thickness and normalized AUC were significant after contralateral subtraction for outer retinal and outer nuclear layer measurements at the lesion level, whereas absolute correlations were nonsignificant; only the former remained significant at the mouse level. Alda-1 and Daidzin differed in subtype composition. Mouse-clustered models indicated lower scores, greater outer nuclear layer first-point thickness, and larger margin angles with Alda-1, but mouse-level comparisons were nonsignificant. Normalized AUC and its contralateral differences showed no significant treatment differences at either level. This framework integrates qualitative, semiquantitative, and quantitative assessments to characterize OCT-visible structural features in mouse retinal laser injury models.

title: Ring-based OCT protocol for retinal ganglion cell complex thickness analysis in mice.
abstract: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) enables non-invasive, high-resolution imaging of retinal layers and is widely used to assess structural changes in preclinical models of retinal and optic nerve disease. However, OCT-based retinal thickness measurements in rodents remain insufficiently standardized, with differences in measurement location and segmentation methodology potentially limiting reproducibility and comparability across studies. We describe a standardized OCT-based protocol for ganglion cell complex (GCC) thickness measurement in mice using predefined retinal landmarks and manual segmentation. Six radial OCT scans separated by 30° are acquired around the optic nerve head, and GCC thickness is measured using ImageJ at three nominal radial distances on each side of the optic nerve: 1000, 1500, and 2000 μm. The applicability of the protocol was evaluated in a murine optic nerve crush (ONC) model. GCC thickness decreased significantly over time, from 68.8 ± 5.2 μm at baseline to 60.7 ± 8.0 μm at day 15 and 60.6 ± 9.8 μm at day 24. Radius- and quadrant-specific analyses further demonstrated the ability of the protocol to detect regional patterns of GCC thinning. This protocol provides a structured approach for OCT-based GCC thickness assessment in mice and may improve consistency and comparability across preclinical studies.

title: Adiposity measures in relation to cognitive screening performance and MRI-derived brain age gap in middle-aged and older adults.
abstract: Background Adiposity has pernicious health implications, notably contributing to cognitive decline and neuroanatomical alterations. Research regarding which measures of adiposity are most related to cognition and the brain is inconsistent. This study explores the relationships between 1) multiple adiposity measures, 2) adiposity measures and cognitive screening performance, and 3) adiposity measures and a machine-learning predicted brain age gap (BAG). Methods Cross-sectional data were combined from two multi-site studies, including 641 non-Hispanic black and non-Hispanic white adults (45-85 years old). Adiposity measures included Body Mass Index (BMI), waist circumference (WC), waist-to-hip ratio (WHpR), waist-to-height ratio (WHtR), and A Body Shape Index (ABSI) z-score. Cognition was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). MoCA scores were converted to equivalent MMSE scores. The predicted BAG was obtained using DeepBrainNet (n = 204) from T1-weighted brain MRI. Results Adiposity measures were significantly correlated, except for BMI and ABSI. After covariate adjustment, cognitive screening associations were small and inconsistent, with a linear association for BMI and nonlinear associations for WC and WHtR. BAG associations depended on model form, with nonlinear patterns for BMI, WC, and WHtR and higher predicted BAG at higher versus intermediate adiposity levels. Combining adiposity measures showed little additional predictive value. Conclusions Anthropometric adiposity measures, particularly BMI, WC, and WHtR, were more consistently related to MRI-derived brain age gap than to brief cognitive screening performance in a cohort of middle-aged and older adults. These findings describe cross-sectional associations with older predicted brain age, especially at higher adiposity levels.

title: PSMA PET Before Prostate Biopsy: From Lesion Detection to Biopsy Avoidance.
abstract: Introduction Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography (PET) may refine biopsy selection when magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is equivocal or nonsuspicious despite persistent clinical concern. This review aims to examine the prospective evidence and to distinguish diagnostic accuracy from biopsy avoidance. Methods Selected prospective cohorts and randomized trials evaluating PSMA PET before prostate biopsy were synthesized narratively, alongside relevant systematic reviews and guidelines. Interpretation focused on patient selection, clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) definitions, biopsy protocols, and verification of PET-negative findings. Results Combining PSMA PET with MRI improves sensitivity and negative predictive value in several prospective studies, particularly in men with equivocal findings. PET-targeted biopsy can improve sampling, but this does not establish the safety of omitting biopsy. In PRIMARY2, a PET-guided pathway achieved noninferior csPCa detection compared with systematic biopsy (12% versus 16%; prespecified noninferiority margin, 10 percentage points), while 49% of men in the PET arm avoided biopsy within 6 months. PET-negative men did not undergo routine immediate biopsy, so the trial does not establish histologically verified negative predictive value. Study heterogeneity and limited follow-up constrain generalization. Conclusions PSMA PET may complement MRI in selected men with residual diagnostic uncertainty. Broader implementation requires validated clinical thresholds, longer follow-up after biopsy deferral, and evidence of cost-effectiveness.

title: Three-dimensional deep-learning age estimation from the fourth rib on high-resolution CT: An evaluative likelihood-ratio approach.
abstract: For four decades, age estimation from the fourth rib has rested on İşcan's visual phase system, which requires the physical bone and returns an ordinal category, not a calibrated probability. We developed a three-dimensional deep-learning pipeline, automated downstream of AI-assisted segmentation, that estimates age from the whole rib on computed tomography (CT) and reports a likelihood ratio. Right fourth ribs from thin-section (1 mm) chest CT of 453 living adults (225 men, 228 women; 18.0-99.8 years) were segmented, posed canonically and encoded as four representations: metric multi-view RGB-D renderings and a point cloud of the sternal end, a point cloud of the complete rib, and twenty morphometric scalars. Sex-specific networks trained by label-distribution learning were evaluated on a frozen hold-out set (three seeds). The selected estimators reached a mean absolute error of 10.6 years in men and 10.4 in women (45-46% below a mean-age predictor; 9.0 and 8.4 years between ages 18 and 70). Likelihood ratios were informative at every threshold from 30 to 70 years (Cllr < 1), sex was classified with an area under the ROC curve of 0.966, and intra-observer reproducibility was ICC 0.872, limited chiefly by the canonical pose. The age signal was not confined to the sternal extremity examined by phase scoring: in women the complete rib outperformed the sternal end (10.4 versus 14.6 years); in men the two were equivalent, consistent with sex-specific standards. Because 1 mm sections cannot resolve İşcan's fine relief, higher-resolution surface capture is a priority for future work.

title: An Anatomical Study of the Middle Hepatic Vein in Close Proximity to the Cystic Plate and Its Underappreciated Clinical Significance in Laparoscopic Hepatectomy (with Video).
abstract: The middle hepatic vein (MHV) is a key landmark for anatomical liver resection, but its peripheral relationship to the cystic plate has mainly been considered a bleeding hazard during cholecystectomy. We examined this relationship and its potential utility as an early landmark during caudal-approach laparoscopic hepatectomy. Fifty-six patients undergoing laparoscopic liver resection involving the main portal fissure between August 2020 and September 2022 were retrospectively reviewed. The shortest distance between the MHV or its nearest branch and the cystic plate was assessed using preoperative CT and three-dimensional reconstruction and categorized as ≤1mm or >1mm. Two hepatobiliary surgeons independently reviewed the imaging findings. In patients with a branch within 1mm, intraoperative identification and tracing to the main MHV were assessed. The closest MHV branch was within 1mm of the cystic plate in 12 patients (21%) and >1mm in 44 (79%). Interobserver classification agreed in 55 of 56 patients (98.2%; Cohen's κ=0.95). In all 12 patients with a branch within 1mm, the corresponding branch was identified at the anticipated intraoperative location without injury and successfully traced to the main MHV. An MHV branch lies immediately beneath the cystic plate in approximately one-fifth of patients. When identified preoperatively, it may represent both a vascular structure at risk of injury and a potential anatomical starting point for tracing the main MHV during a caudal approach. Comparative studies are needed to determine its effect on operative efficiency or safety.

title: [Place of clinical breast examination in breast cancer screening strategies. French College of Gynecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF) recommendations for clinical practice].
abstract: France, like many countries around the world, is facing a rise in the incidence of breast cancer. Numerous studies have shown that the risk of death is linked to the initial stage of the tumor. In this context, mammographic screening for breast cancer aims to diagnose cancers at a subclinical stage, to limit treatment-related morbidity and reduce mortality. In France, this screening is recommended every two years for women aged 50 to 74, while clinical breast examination (CBE) by a healthcare professional is recommended by the Haute Autorité de Santé (HAS) starting at age 25, to be performed annually with no upper age limit. However, the practice of CBE needs to be updated, particularly regarding its impact on the number of cancers diagnosed, their stage, and mortality, considering new data from international literature. Design The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) method was used to assess the quality of the evidence on which these recommendations were based. Methods The Senology Commission (SC) of the French College of Gynecologists and Obstetricians examined 16 questions regarding CBE, distinguishing four groups of women (the general population with or without mammography screening, women over 70 years of age, high or very-risk women, and women previously treated for breast cancer). For each scenario, it was determined whether performing a CBE, compared with not performing it, led to the detection of more breast cancers, reduced tumor size, or improved survival. One question addressed the training requirements for CBE. Results The SC issued three recommendations aimed at: 1) recommending annual CBE for women in the general population aged 30 to 74, 2) recommending annual CBE for women who have previously been treated for breast cancer, 3) recommending that CBE be performed by a trained healthcare professional. The SC issued four position statements aimed at: 1) not advising CBE for women in the general population under the age of 30, as the procedure carries a risk of unnecessary follow-up tests in a group of women where the incidence of breast cancer is very low. 2) advising performing a CBE during breast cancer screening; 3) advising an annual CBE for women over 75 years of age, with the discontinuation of this practice depending on comorbidities and life expectancy. 4) advising annual CBE for women at high and very high-risk starting at age 20. According to the experts of the CNGOF's Scientific Committee, a CBE should be performed only after obtaining explicit consent following the provision of information on its benefits and risks. The SC urges all women who notice a change or abnormality in their breasts to consult their doctor without delay to undergo a clinical breast exam.

The SC issued four position statements aimed at: 1) not advising CBE for women in the general population under the age of 30, as the procedure carries a risk of unnecessary follow-up tests in a group of women where the incidence of breast cancer is very low. 2) advising performing a CBE during breast cancer screening; 3) advising an annual CBE for women over 75 years of age, with the discontinuation of this practice depending on comorbidities and life expectancy. 4) advising annual CBE for women at high and very high-risk starting at age 20. According to the experts of the CNGOF's Scientific Committee, a CBE should be performed only after obtaining explicit consent following the provision of information on its benefits and risks. The SC urges all women who notice a change or abnormality in their breasts to consult their doctor without delay to undergo a clinical breast exam.

title: Prognostic Value of Late Gadolinium Enhancement in Non-Ischemic Dilated Cardiomyopathy: A Prospective Observational Study from India.
abstract: Background Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (NIDCM) represents a significant cause of heart failure and sudden cardiac death (SCD). Current risk stratification relies heavily on left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), which has limitations in predicting adverse outcomes. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging may provide additional prognostic information. Methods This prospective observational study enrolled 88 consecutive NIDCM patients who underwent CMR imaging at our institution. Patients were followed for a minimum of 6 months and thereafter until a common study closure date, giving a mean follow-up of 337±173 days. The primary endpoint was a composite of major adverse cardiac events (MACE), defined as sudden cardiac death, heart failure death, aborted sudden cardiac death, sustained ventricular tachycardia, and heart failure hospitalization. Results LGE was present in 44 patients (50%). The most common pattern was mid-myocardial enhancement (40.9%), followed by a combination of patterns (25.0%) and transmural enhancement (22.7%); the interventricular septum was the most frequently involved segment (81.8%). MACE occurred in 22.7% of LGE-positive patients versus 13.6% of LGE-negative patients. ROC curve analysis identified LGE extent >26% of LV volume as the optimal threshold for predicting MACE (sensitivity 70%, specificity 73.5%, AUC 0.75). Patients with LGE >26% had significantly higher event rates (43.7% vs 10.7%; unadjusted OR 6.48, 95% CI 1.45-28.9; p=0.02). Conclusions Greater LGE extent was associated with adverse cardiac events in NIDCM patients. CMR-based risk stratification may help identify high-risk patients who could benefit from ICD, but external validation in larger cohorts is required before using this threshold clinically.

title: Electron-beam-crosslinked injectable poly-γ-glutamic acid hydrogels: Physicochemical properties, long-term in vivo retention, and biocompatibility.
abstract: Injectable hydrogels for biomedical applications require controllable mechanical properties, sustained in vivo retention, and favorable biocompatibility. Here, injectable poly-γ-glutamic acid (γ-PGA) hydrogels were prepared by electron-beam (EB) irradiation at 30 kGy (low dose, LD), 150 kGy (medium dose, MD), and 200 kGy (high dose, HD), without additional chemical crosslinking agents. Nuclear magnetic resonance and Fourier-transform infrared analyses revealed irradiation-induced spectral changes in γ-PGA. Physicochemical and mechanical characterization demonstrated distinct differences in swelling behavior, gel fraction, rheological properties, and injection force among the irradiation groups. In vivo retention and biocompatibility were assessed in mice over 180 days following subcutaneous injection. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based volumetric analysis showed progressively prolonged retention from LD to HD, with γ-PGA (LD) remaining detectable through day 7, γ-PGA (MD) through day 150, and γ-PGA (HD) retaining 74.26 ± 3.77% of its initial volume on day 180. Higher irradiation levels were also associated with greater G' and G″ values and reduced maximum swelling. Compared with the hyaluronic acid hydrogel, the γ-PGA hydrogels exhibited less pronounced early post-injection volume expansion, while their long-term MRI-detectable volume profiles varied among the irradiation groups. No marked local or systemic adverse responses were detected based on MRI, histological observations, serum cytokine analysis, hematologic assessment, body weight monitoring, and relative organ weight measurements. Overall, EB irradiation enabled the preparation of injectable γ-PGA hydrogels with irradiation-dependent physicochemical and rheological properties, prolonged in vivo retention, practical injectability, and favorable biocompatibility.

title: Silent brain infarction and clinical outcomes in rheumatic mitral stenosis: A prospective cohort study.
abstract: Rheumatic mitral stenosis (MS) affects a relatively young population. Thromboembolic risk in MS is traditionally attributed to atrial fibrillation (AF), although silent brain infarction (SBI) may occur in sinus rhythm. Further, the contribution of underlying atrial disease independent of rhythm remains uncertain. To determine the prevalence and correlates of SBI and evaluate associations with subsequent cerebrovascular and clinical outcomes. In this prospective cohort, 211 adults with moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS underwent baseline brain MRI, echocardiography, biomarker assessment, and rhythm evaluation. Firth penalized logistic regression was used for SBI and longitudinal outcomes. Clinical follow-up was available in 194 patients. SBI was present in 44 patients (20.9%). SBI occurred in 25.4% with AF and 18.6% in sinus rhythm (unadjusted OR 1.49, 95% CI 0.70-3.10; p = 0.284); adjusted AF was not significantly associated with SBI (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.37-1.76; p = 0.605). Each doubling of BNP was associated with SBI overall (OR 1.34, 95% CI 1.01-1.82; p = 0.040) and in sinus rhythm (OR 1.56, 95% CI 1.12-2.27; p = 0.007). During follow-up, 15 patients developed stroke/TIA; baseline SBI was associated with subsequent stroke/TIA (17.1% vs 5.2%; adjusted OR 3.40, 95% CI 1.14-9.96; p = 0.029). BNP was associated with stroke/death (49 events; OR per doubling 1.45, 95% CI 1.09-2.00; p = 0.010) and death (40 events; OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.14-2.25; p = 0.005), but not stroke/TIA. SBI is common in rheumatic MS and identifies patients at higher subsequent cerebrovascular risk. BNP is associated with SBI and broader adverse prognosis, particularly mortality. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require further validation.

title: Pleural empyema and perisplenic abscess caused by Clostridioides difficile in a patient with liver cirrhosis and previous C. difficile colitis: a case report.
abstract: Background Clostridioides difficile is a leading cause of healthcare-associated diarrhea, whereas extraintestinal infection is rare and pleural involvement is exceptional, with only a handful of cases reported to date. Patients with liver cirrhosis are at increased risk of bacterial infection and of C. difficile infection, but C. difficile pleural empyema has been reported only once in this population. Case presentation A 43-year-old man with alcohol-related liver cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class C) and C. difficile colitis two years earlier was admitted with hepatic decompensation and a C-reactive protein of 151 mg/L, without gastrointestinal symptoms. Computed tomography showed a large left-sided pleural collection. The aspirate contained 6,870 cells/µL with 94.2% granulocytes and had a pH of 6.97, consistent with empyema. Piperacillin/tazobactam was started empirically and empyemectomy was performed. Intraoperative swabs yielded C. difficile on MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and toxin PCR was positive; histopathology showed acute purulent pleuritis. Two weeks later the empyema recurred and a new perisplenic collection appeared; C. difficile toxin was again detected at both sites. Treatment was escalated to meropenem, vancomycin and metronidazole, combined with repeat surgical evacuation and percutaneous drainage. Repeated stool testing for C. difficile antigen and toxin remained negative. After a prolonged intensive care stay requiring tracheostomy, the patient recovered and was discharged to a rehabilitation facility. Conclusions C. difficile should be considered as a cause of pleural empyema, particularly in patients with liver cirrhosis and previous C. difficile infection. Recovery of C. difficile from extraintestinal specimens should not be dismissed as contamination; timely source control combined with targeted antimicrobial therapy is essential for a favorable outcome.

title: Clinical utility of computed tomography angiography in assessing internal maxillary artery position during temporomandibular joint ankylosis surgery.
abstract: Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) ankylosis surgery carries a high risk of intraoperative bleeding due to the close anatomical relationship between the ankylotic mass and the internal maxillary artery (IMA). Although computed tomography angiography (CTA) is widely used for preoperative vascular assessment, its reliability in predicting the intraoperative IMA course in TMJ ankylosis surgery remains uncertain. This exploratory prospective case series included 34 patients (22 males, 12 females; mean age 19.6 ± 2.5 years) with TMJ ankylosis involving 48 joints treated with 1 cm gap arthroplasty. CTA identified three IMA-ankylotic mass relationships: close contact (n = 20, further subdivided into medial, n = 8; posterior, n = 12), enclosed (n = 13), and no contact (n = 15). Overall concordance between preoperative CTA-based IMA classification and intraoperative findings was 56.3%, with discordance in 43.7% of joints (Cramér's V = 0.069; P = 0.97). Concordance varied across CTA categories, with the lowest concordance observed in the no contact group (53.3%). Despite differences in preoperative CTA-based IMA classification, intraoperative outcomes did not differ significantly among groups. Ankylotic mass resection time was comparable across categories (median 23-24 min; P = 0.085), and no significant differences were observed in estimated blood loss, vascular control measures, or blood transfusion requirements. In conclusion, CTA demonstrates limited concordance with the clinically observed intraoperative course of the IMA in TMJ ankylosis surgery and does not significantly stratify intraoperative outcomes. Therefore, it may be considered a complementary tool for preoperative planning rather than a definitive predictor of intraoperative vascular anatomy.

Ankylotic mass resection time was comparable across categories (median 23-24 min; P = 0.085), and no significant differences were observed in estimated blood loss, vascular control measures, or blood transfusion requirements. In conclusion, CTA demonstrates limited concordance with the clinically observed intraoperative course of the IMA in TMJ ankylosis surgery and does not significantly stratify intraoperative outcomes. Therefore, it may be considered a complementary tool for preoperative planning rather than a definitive predictor of intraoperative vascular anatomy.

title: Classification and surgical treatment of temporomandibular joint calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease: a single-center case series.
abstract: This study aimed to classify calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease of the temporomandibular joint and evaluate the therapeutic outcomes. Surgically treated patients from January 2020 to September 2025 were classified into three types based on lesion location and extent. Type I involved the superior compartment with or without skull base destruction. Type II affected the inferior compartment with or without condylar destruction. Type III involved both compartments affecting the condyle and skull base. Treatments included complete excision and reconstruction using autologous or alloplastic materials. Maximum interincisal opening and visual analogue scale pain scores were evaluated preoperatively and at follow-ups of at least 6 months, while computed tomography assessed recurrence and reconstruction. Ten patients (mean age of 57.2 years) were included, comprising four in type I, four in type II, and two in type III. Bone invasion occurred in eight patients. Reconstruction procedures involved autologous tissues, such as temporalis myofascial flaps or coronoid grafts in three patients, and alloplastic materials in five. The mean follow-up duration was 25.1 months. Maximum (range) interincisal opening was improved from 33.0 mm (23.0-48.0) to 39.5 mm (37.0-45.0) (P < 0.05). Pain scores decreased from 6.0 (2.0-8.0) to 0.0 (0.0-1.0) (P < 0.05). One patient had coronoid process graft resorption without malocclusion. No recurrence, screw loosening, or implant displacement occurred. TMJ CPPD can be classified and treated according to the lesion location and extension. Complete excision and reconstruction are associated with low recurrence.

title: TTA-MVUM: A Tumor and Text-Aware Multi-View Mamba Framework for Clinical Target Volume Auto-Segmentation in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma Radiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose Accurate segmentation of clinical target volumes (CTV) is critical for the success of radiotherapy in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Manual contouring is time-consuming and prone to considerable inter-observer variability. Current auto-segmentation models rely exclusively on images, which may lead to sub-optimal accuracy. This study sought to substantially improve CTV auto-segmentation by incorporating tumor and clinical text information with multimodal deep learning. Methods and materials We retrospectively collected data from 184 NPC patients treated at our institution, with 144 cases allocated for model training and 40 for test. We propose a tumor- and text-aware multi-view UMamba (TTA-MVUM) model with text-image cross-attention modules to fuse visual and textual features. The model input comprised CT images, manually contoured primary gross tumor volume and metastatic lymph nodes, structured text contouring plan extracted by a large language model from electronic health records. Training was guided by a composite loss integrating Dice, cross-entropy and contrastive terms. Model performance was evaluated using Dice, 95% Hausdorff distance and averaged surface distance. Results The proposed TTA-MVUM model significantly outperformed state-of-the-art image-only and tumor-aware baselines, yielding mean Dice of 0.892 ± 0.035 for high-risk CTV, 0.738 ± 0.149 for low-risk CTV, and 0.889 ± 0.024 for the entire CTV, respectively, with similar improvements for other metrics. Using either tumor information or clinical text alone also surpassed baseline models, but performance remained inferior to the combined approach. Conclusions Integrating tumor priors and text guidance can substantially improve the NPC CTV auto-segmentation accuracy and clinical applicability.

title: Neoadjuvant Chemoradiotherapy with Modern Bowel-Sparing Intensity-Modulated Radiotherapy for Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: A Multicenter Single-Arm Phase II Trial.
abstract: Purpose The study evaluated the risk of grade ≥2 acute diarrhea of modern bowel-sparing intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT)-based neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) versus three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy (3DCRT)-based nCRT. Materials and methods In this open-label, historically controlled, multicenter, single-arm phase II trial, patients with LARC, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-2, and adequate organ function were recruited. Protocol treatment involved concurrent capecitabine and IMRT, consisting of 45 Gy (25 fractions) for elective nodes and an optional 5.4 Gy (3 fractions) boost for gross disease. Bowel-sparing constraints included small-bowel volume receiving 15 Gy (V15Gy) of <200 cc. Acute toxicities were graded in the protocol-defined primary outcome window. Grade ≥2 acute diarrhea was tested against a 26% historical benchmark from phase II trials of 3DCRT-based nCRT with capecitabine with a one-sided α-level of 0.05 and 80% power. Results Fifty-five patients were enrolled, including 48 patients with stage III disease and 25 patients with a positive circumferential resection margin on magnetic resonance imaging. Fifty-four patients (98.2%) completed protocol-defined nCRT. The median small-bowel V15Gy was 85 cc (interquartile range, 47-105). Grade ≥2 acute diarrhea occurred in four patients (7.3%; 90% confidence interval, 2.5-15.9; p < 0.001) in the intention-to-treat cohort. Fifty patients underwent radical surgery, and the pathological complete response and circumferential resection margin >1 mm rates were 6.0% and 88.0%, respectively, with grade ≥2 postoperative complications observed in 14% of patients. After median follow-up of 14 months, the 12-month locoregional progression-free and overall survival rates were 95.0% and 98.2%, respectively. Conclusions Modern bowel-sparing IMRT in nCRT for LARC was associated with a low rate of grade ≥2 acute diarrhea with no obvious unfavorable signals for resectability, locoregional control, or safety; however, longer follow-up is needed to assess mature oncologic outcomes and late toxicities.

title: Prevalence of Muscle loss during and after Pelvic Radiotherapy in Gynecological Cancer Patients.
abstract: Introduction Women undergoing pelvic radiotherapy are at risk of developing sarcopenia, defined by muscle loss. In patients treated with radiotherapy for cervical cancer, post-treatment muscle loss has been associated with poorer cancer-specific and overall survival. This study aimed to longitudinally assess sarcopenia and changes in muscle during radiotherapy and follow-up, and to evaluate whether bioelectrical impedance analysis can serve as an accurate bedside alternative to computed tomography (CT) for sarcopenia assessment. Methods and materials This prospective cohort study included women with histologically confirmed primary cervical, endometrial, vulvar, or vaginal cancer, all scheduled to undergo external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) with curative intent. Sarcopenia was assessed at baseline, during the last week of EBRT, and at the three- and six-month follow-up. Two methods were used to evaluate sarcopenia: lumbar skeletal muscle index measured via CT scan (gold standard) and appendicular skeletal muscle mass via bioelectrical impedance analysis. Fisher's exact test and the Mann-Whitney U test were used to compare baseline characteristics between women with and without sarcopenia during the last week of radiotherapy. Results A total of 31 women were included. Based on CT scans, the prevalence of sarcopenia was 23% at baseline, 32% at the last week of radiotherapy, and 42% at the three-month follow-up. At the six-month follow-up, 29% of the women were sarcopenic. Bioelectrical impedance analysis detected sarcopenia in only 0% to 50% of cases across the various time points. Patients with FIGO stage III were significantly more frequently sarcopenic based on their appendicular skeletal muscle index as assessed by CT scan during the last week of EBRT. Conclusions The prevalence of sarcopenia is high in women treated with radiotherapy for gynecological cancer. An increase in the prevalence of sarcopenia was observed, reaching its highest point at the three-month follow-up. Sarcopenia may be underestimated when assessed using bioelectrical impedance analysis, as indicated by the low sensitivity observed.

title: The Complementary Impact of Amino Acid PET with Diffusion and Perfusion MRI for Glioblastoma Tumor Delineation.
abstract: Background While standard MRI imaging is known to underestimate glioblastoma tumor extent, advanced imaging techniques including 18-FDOPA PET, dynamic contrast enhanced (DCE) perfusion MRI, and diffusion weighted MRI (DWI) have been utilized on clinical trials to identify tumor within and beyond gadolinium enhancement for radiation targeting. This clinical trial analysis quantifies how DCE, DWI and 18-FDOPA PET identify tumor beyond standard imaging, and whether these techniques are complementary and feasible. Methods Patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma enrolled on a phase II clinical trial underwent pre-radiation 18-FDOPA PET/CT, DCE, DWI, and standard MRI sequences. Tumor volumes were separately delineated using each imaging modality and incorporated into radiation target volumes, and were compared for overlapping and non-overlapping segments. Results In 153 enrolled patients included in this analysis, tumor was identified beyond conventionally used radiation volume expansions of 5-, 10-, 15-, and 20 mm from standard MRI tumor volumes in 86%, 56%, 38% and 20% of patients, respectively. Advanced imaging techniques identified partially overlapping tumor volumes; PET identified tumor outside of the advanced MRI subvolumes in 88%, while DWI and DCE identified tumor outside of standard MRI and PET in 95% cases, indicating these imaging techniques are complementary. Conclusions Advanced imaging techniques including DCE, DWI, and 18-FDOPA PET allow complementary delineation of glioblastoma beyond contrast-enhancing tumor from standard MRI, and may be most valuable when used in combination. These advanced imaging methods can potentially facilitate accurate tumor targeting with reduced CTV expansions to spare normal tissue and enable safe hypofractionated radiation therapy.

title: RESPONSE-ADAPTIVE STEREOTACTIC BODY RADIOTHERAPY BOOST AFTER CONCURRENT CHEMORADIOTHERAPY IN UNRESECTABLE STAGE III NSCLC: A PROSPECTIVE SINGLE-CENTRE COHORT STUDY.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to escalate the dose to the residual primary tumor with an adaptive stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) boost after concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) in unresectable stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and to explore, within this cohort, whether a higher cumulative dose to the residual primary was associated with better locoregional control (LRC) and whether this translated into a difference in overall survival (OS). Materials and methods In this single-center, prospective, single-arm cohort, 51 patients received concurrent CRT (50 Gy/25 fractions with weekly carboplatin and paclitaxel) followed by an adaptive boost (30 Gy/5 fractions to the residual primary, 10 Gy/5 fractions to residual nodes), without consolidation durvalumab. Doses were summed by deformable registration and reported as EQD2. Response was assessed at 3 months with FDG-PET/CT (PERCIST), and toxicity with CTCAE v5.0. Outcomes estimated by Kaplan-Meier; predictors by Cox regression. Results At a median follow-up of 26 months, 2-year OS and LRC were 61.5% and 62.8%. The median PFS and DMFS were 13 and 16 months, and distant metastasis was the dominant failure pattern (41.2%). Cumulative dose below 94.77 Gy (EQD2) to the residual primary independently predicted worse LRC (HR 5.86), and a 3-month locoregional SUVmax ≥4.55 predicted worse LRC (HR 5.04). OS was independently associated with residual nodal volume, 3-month metabolic progression, and subsequent locoregional progression. Grade 3-4 pneumonitis occurred in 7.8%, grade 3 esophagitis in one patient (2%), and hemoptysis in five (9.8%). Conclusion The SBRT boost achieved encouraging locoregional control, including in bulky and node-advanced disease, without immunotherapy, and higher cumulative dose to the residual primary was associated with better locoregional control. Hemoptysis was the main safety concern and occurred predominantly in patients with pre-existing hemoptysis, supporting careful selection and strict bronchial constraints. Local escalation alone did not overcome the competing risk of distant failure.

title: Long-term preservation of normal brain tissue by minibeam radiation therapy does not require mature T cells.
abstract: Minibeam radiation therapy (MBRT) preserves normal tissue while maintaining antitumour efficacy, yet the mechanisms underlying this remarkable normal tissue tolerance remain poorly understood. Although adaptive immune responses have been implicated in the antitumour effects of spatially fractionated radiotherapy, their contribution to normal tissue preservation remains unknown. Here, we used a loss-of-function model to determine whether mature T cells are required for the expression of the long-term normal tissue-sparing phenotype associated with MBRT. Immunocompetent Fischer 344 rats and athymic nude rats received X-ray MBRT or conventional radiotherapy (CRT) at a mean dose of 30 Gy and were followed for up to six months. Long-term normal tissue response was assessed using complementary behavioural analyses, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and histopathological evaluation of immune infiltration, vascular integrity, glial activation and neuronal survival. Nude rats developed beam-path alopecia and skin lesions earlier than immunocompetent rats and showed a transient reduction in cortical CD31 staining at 7 days post-irradiation, indicating greater acute radiosensitivity without mature T cells. Beyond this early window, the long-term phenotype was comparable between strains: no MRI-detectable lesions, no neuronal loss and no sustained glial activation at 6 months. MBRT induced modest late reductions in exploratory behaviour and recognition memory in both strains, with no significant strain × irradiation interaction. Histologically, MBRT elicited a moderate and transient CD3+ T-cell infiltration that resolved within seven days, whereas CRT induced a stronger and more sustained inflammatory response. Mature T cells modulate the acute tissue reaction to MBRT but are not required for the long-term normal tissue-sparing phenotype. Within the sensitivity of this study, powered for large effects only, mature T cells are unlikely to be a major determinant of long-term MBRT tissue preservation, redirecting attention towards innate immune, vascular and stromal processes.

title: Intraoperative visualization with 3D fluoroscopy for posterior pelvic fixation is associated with lower cumulative imaging-related radiation exposure.
abstract: Introduction Achieving optimal screw positioning in posterior pelvic ring (PR) fracture fixation is critical for fracture stability and safety. Formerly, our institution used intraoperative plain-film fluoroscopy followed by postoperative computed tomography (CT) to assess fracture reduction and screw placement. Introduction of the 3D mobile C-arm enables immediate volumetric intraoperative assessment, may improve intraoperative visualization, and may alter conventional imaging requirements. This study compared cumulative imaging-related radiation exposure between cases performed with intraoperative 3D fluoroscopy (3DF) against standard intraoperative plain-film fluoroscopy (2DF), including postoperative CT utilization. Methods A retrospective review was conducted on patients treated for posterior PR fractures at a level 1 trauma center between 2014 and 2023. Utilization of 3DF or plain-film fluoroscopy, and any intraoperative screw changes were documented. Rates and details of postoperative complications and subsequent reoperations were recorded for patients with > 3 months follow-up. Radiation doses for 3DF, 2DF, and postoperative CT were extracted from radiology reports. Results Among 245 patients (mean age 47.2, 52.2% male) undergoing fixation for posterior PR fractures, 89 (36.3%) had 3DF intraoperatively, while 156 (63.7%) had 2DF. 27 patients (8 3DF, 19 2DF, p = 0.443) had screws changed intraoperatively, primarily to modify screw path (n = 16, 59.3%), to achieve better purchase/reduction (n = 5, 18.5%), to modify screw size (n = 3, 11.1%), to change screw type (n = 2, 7.4%), and failure to advance screw (n = 1, 3.7%). Mean radiation dose for the 3DF group was significantly lower (179.2 mGy vs 526.1 mGy, p < 0.001). When excluding postoperative CT dose (n = 194), intraoperative-only radiation remained lower with 3DF (median 79.1 (IQR 51.5-148.7) vs 318.0 (IQR 71.6-751.5) mGy; p < 0.001). Among 119 patients with > 3 months follow-up, reoperation was less frequent with 3DF (9.5% vs 31.2%, p = 0.012), predominantly for symptomatic implant removal. Discussion and conclusion Intraoperative 3DF was associated with lower cumulative radiation exposure compared to traditional fluoroscopy with routine postoperative CT, and intraoperative dose alone was also lower. Reoperation was less frequent in the 3DF group, but most reoperations were implant removals for symptomatic or planned indications. These findings highlight the potential of 3DF as a practical radiation efficient quality assurance tool in posterior pelvic fixation.

title: Machine Learning Reveals Prognostic Value of Medical History in Suspected Coronary Artery Disease.
abstract: Background Risk stratification in suspected coronary artery disease (CAD) relies on clinical history and imaging, but longitudinal medical history may provide additional prognostic information. Objectives This study evaluated whether machine learning models using 10-year historical registry data improves prediction of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) beyond demographics and stress perfusion cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) in patients with suspected CAD. Methods A total of 2,159 patients (65 ± 12 years, 44% women) undergoing stress perfusion CMR were included. Models used demographics, CMR findings, and registry diagnoses and procedures from the prior 10 years. MACE was defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or coronary intervention. Random Forest models were used for binary prediction, and Random Survival Forests (RSF) and penalized Ridge Cox regression for time-to-event analysis. Results During 2.7 ± 0.9 years of follow-up, 212 patients (9.8%) experienced MACE. For binary prediction, the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.66 (95% CI: 0.62-0.69) using demographics and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.68-0.75; P = 0.001) after adding historical registry data. The full model achieved an AUROC of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.79-0.85) and outperformed the demographics-plus-CMR model (AUROC: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.78-0.84; ΔAUROC: 0.014; 95% CI: 0.002-0.027; P = 0.029). In time-to-event analysis, RSF and Cox regression performed similarly using demographics and CMR (concordance index [C-index] 0.80 for both; P = 0.546). After including registry data RSF achieved a C-index of 0.81 (P = 0.144), and Cox performance decreased to C-index 0.77 (P < 0.001). Conclusions In patients with suspected CAD, machine learning models using 10-year historical registry data have the potential to improve prognostic risk prediction beyond demographics and stress perfusion CMR.

title: Heart Failure Phenotyping and Prognosis by CMR-Derived Oxygen Delivery and Extraction.
abstract: Heart failure reflects impaired matching of systemic oxygen delivery to metabolic demand, yet resting oxygen transport is seldom measured. The purpose of this study was to noninvasively derive resting oxygen delivery and extraction using cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) and relate these to clinical characteristics and outcomes. In this retrospective study, in patients with heart failure referred for clinical CMR, cardiac output was assessed by cine imaging; basal blood-pool T2 mapping provided imaging-derived venous oxygen saturation; and measured hemoglobin enabled calculation of arterial oxygen content. Arterial oxygen saturation was fixed at 96%. We derived indexed systemic oxygen delivery (DO2i), oxygen extraction fraction (OEF), and indexed systemic oxygen consumption (VO2i). The endpoint was all-cause death or heart failure hospitalization. A total of 429 patients were included (62 events). VO2i varied widely (tertile means 138.8, 207.9, and 293.8 mL/min/m2), while left ventricular ejection fraction did not differ (38.8%, 40.6%, and 40.3%; P = 0.42). Imaging-derived venous oxygen saturation decreased across increasing VO2i tertiles (61.5%, 54.3%, and 50.7%; P < 0.0001). In Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, ejection fraction, and late gadolinium enhancement, VO2i was associated with the endpoint (HR: 1.15 per 50 mL/min/m2, 95% CI: 1.00-1.32; P = 0.046), but discrimination of VO2i alone was poor (Harrell's C = 0.53). Delivery-extraction phenotypes differed in event risk (log-rank P = 0.026): event proportions were 8.6% (high DO2i/low OEF), 14.0% (low DO2i/low OEF), 16.8% (high DO2i/high OEF), and 18.3% (low DO2i/high OEF). The delivery-extraction phenotype remained associated with outcome after adjustment for age, sex, left ventricular ejection fraction, and CMR-derived filling pressure. In this hypothesis-generating study, CMR-based oxygen supply-demand assessment delineates resting delivery-extraction phenotypes associated with heart failure outcomes.

title: Management of Coronary Calcified Nodules: A Position Statement.
abstract: Coronary calcified nodules are an uncommon but important substrate for acute coronary syndromes, stent underexpansion, and recurrent target lesion revascularization. This consensus integrates pathologic, imaging, prognostic, and interventional evidence to guide practical decision-making. Intravascular imaging is essential for diagnosis, mechanism definition, and procedural optimization. Optical coherence tomography provides superior assessment of cap disruption and thrombus, whereas intravascular ultrasound remains valuable when contrast exposure or lesion crossing limits optical coherence tomography. Treatment should be tailored to lesion crossability, calcium distribution, and the need for mechanical scaffolding. No calcium-modification device or drug-eluting stent vs drug-coated balloon strategy has demonstrated consistent superiority. The proposed type IIa/IIb framework is hypothesis-generating and requires prospective validation. Calcified nodule-related target lesion failure should be managed by correcting the dominant mechanical mechanism before antiproliferative therapy. These recommendations emphasize individualized, imaging-guided percutaneous coronary intervention and identify priorities for prospective comparative research.

title: Transcatheter Solution to Atypical Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Drainage in a Single Ventricle Patient.
abstract: Background Partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) is typically incompatible with single ventricle physiology if left unrepaired before cavopulmonary connection. This report describes a rare anatomical variant and novel interventional solution. Case summary An 8-month-old female with hypoplastic left heart variant developed profound cyanosis following bidirectional Glenn because of unrepaired PAPVD of the right upper pulmonary vein to the superior vena cava (SVC). Retrospective 3-dimensional reconstruction of the patient's neonatal computed tomography angiogram revealed a small interlobar vessel between the anomalous pulmonary vein and the anatomically normal right lower pulmonary vein. This interlobar vessel's gross dilatation and anatomical features permitted percutaneous device occlusion of the PAPVD connection to the SVC, isolating SVC return to the cavopulmonary circulation while preserving unobstructed pulmonary venous return to the atrium. Discussion Surgical and interventional solutions are reviewed in the context of this unusual anatomical variant. Take-home messages In the uncommon circumstance of an unrecognized anomalous pulmonary vein with connections to both systemic and pulmonary venous circulations, consideration may be given to interventional occlusion of the PAPVD connection to the systemic vein. Retrospective application of contemporary 3-dimensional reconstruction tools can add great value in delineating complex or unusual anatomy.

title: Sarcomatoid Renal Cell Carcinoma With Cardiac Metastasis Causing Right Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction.
abstract: Background Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) rarely metastasizes to the heart, and an aggressive histologic transformation known as sarcomatoid dedifferentiation confers a poor prognosis. Case summary A patient presented with progressive exertional dyspnea. Initial laboratory studies revealed elevated troponin and elevated D-dimer. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography showed a right ventricle (RV) filling defect. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a large lobulated mass extending from the RV free wall into the outflow tract, encroaching on the pulmonic valve with an ejection fraction of <20%. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging revealed a right renal mass. The patient suffered a fatal arrest because of obstructive shock from severe RV outflow tract obstruction. Discussion Postmortem examination confirmed metastatic sarcomatoid RCC. Patients typically present with advanced disease, and survival is <1 year. Combination immunotherapy is approved for metastatic RCC. Initiating immunotherapy would not have addressed the patient's acute hemodynamic compromise. Take-home message Early recognition of metastatic RCC is crucial for potential therapeutic intervention, though prognosis remains poor in advanced cases.

title: True Left-Ventricular Aneurysm After Ventricular Tachycardia Ablation: The Role of Imaging in a Rare Complication.
abstract: Background Left ventricular (LV) pseudoaneurysm is an uncommon but recognized complication of ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation. In contrast, true LV aneurysm has been reported only rarely. Case summary Transthoracic echocardiogram, supported by cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging, initially suggested an LV pseudoaneurysm in a patient after VT ablation. During evaluation for percutaneous closure, left ventriculogram and 3-dimensional transesophageal echocardiogram revealed more complex anatomy, prompting referral for surgical repair. Intraoperative findings confirmed a true LV aneurysm. Discussion True LV aneurysm may represent a rare complication of deep radiofrequency energy delivery during catheter ablation resulting in myocardial injury. Because differentiating true aneurysms from pseudoaneurysms can be challenging, a multimodality imaging approach may improve anatomical characterization, guide management, and enhance understanding of the underlying mechanism. Take-home message Multimodality imaging can improve anatomical characterization and procedural planning in patients with the rare complication of true left aneurysm after catheter ablation.

title: Antegrade Dissection and Re-Entry for Recanalization of Traumatic Coronary Artery Dissection.
abstract: Background Traumatic coronary artery dissection (TCAD) is a rare catastrophic complication of blunt chest trauma, often masked by concomitant injuries, posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Case summary A 20-year-old man with polytrauma after a motorcycle accident developed cardiogenic shock. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) suggested occlusive left anterior descending dissection, confirmed by delayed angiography under extracorporeal membrane oxygenation support. Stingray-based antegrade dissection and re-entry (ADR) with cutting balloon fenestration and drug-coated balloon angioplasty achieved TIMI flow grade 3. Three-month follow-up showed favorable left anterior descending healing and improved cardiac function. Discussion CCTA enables early TCAD diagnosis. ADR facilitates guidewire passage, and a stentless strategy is preferable in young polytrauma patients at high bleeding risk. Take-home messages Maintain suspicion for TCAD after blunt chest trauma, especially with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction features. CCTA aids early diagnosis; ADR-based percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-coated balloon is safe and effective.
