title: Efficacy of hysteroscopic curettage and niche resection in type II and III cesarean scar pregnancies.
abstract: Introduction To evaluate the efficacy and safety of hysteroscopic curettage combined with cesarean scar diverticulum canal-opening after focused ultrasound ablation surgery (FUAS) pretreatment in patients with type II and III cesarean scar pregnancy (CSP). Methods Clinical data of 105 patients with type II/III CSP treated between January 2019 and October 2022 were retrospectively analyzed. All patients received FUAS pretreatment. The observation group ( n = 47) underwent hysteroscopic curettage combined with niche canal-opening, while the control group ( n = 58) received hysteroscopic curettage alone. Surgical parameters, postoperative recovery, complications, reintervention rates, and menstrual outcomes were compared. Results The observation group had significantly shorter operation time [20 (15,25) vs. 25 (20,31) min, p = 0.001], less intraoperative blood loss [5 (5,10) vs. 10 (10,50) mL, p = 0.002], lower complication rate [4.3% vs. 17.2%, p = 0.038], and lower reintervention rate [4.3% vs. 19.0%, p = 0.023]. No between-group differences were observed in postoperative hemoglobin decline, hospital stay, vaginal bleeding duration, human chorionic gonadotropin normalization time, menstrual recovery time, or residual scar myometrial thickness (all p > 0.05). Among patients with preoperative prolonged menstruation, menstrual duration improved in both groups ( p < 0.05), with a higher improvement rate in the observation group [75.0% vs. 23.1%, p = 0.005]. Conclusions FUAS pretreatment combined with hysteroscopic surgery is safe and effective for type II/III CSP. Adding diverticulum canal-opening to hysteroscopic curettage further optimized surgical outcomes by reducing operation time, intraoperative blood loss, complication rates, and the need for reintervention, while also significantly improving prolonged menstruation. This combined strategy may serve as an optimized minimally invasive alternative for patients desiring fertility, though long-term reproductive safety requires further verification.

title: Diagnostic performance of MRI, endorectal ultrasound, and FAPI PET/MRI for identifying pathological complete response after short-course radiotherapy and chemoimmunotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer: a retrospective study.
abstract: Background Accurate imaging-based response assessment is essential for proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of MRI, endorectal ultrasound (ERUS) and 18F-FAPI PET/MRI for identifying pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy (SCRT) followed by chemoimmunotherapy. Methods This single-center retrospective study included 143 patients. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy with 95% confidence intervals. Cohen's κ assessed agreement between imaging-defined complete response (iCR) and pCR. Paired comparisons used Cochran's Q and Holm-adjusted exact McNemar tests. Results The pCR rate was 51.0%. MRI ( n = 118), ERUS ( n = 81), and PET/MRI ( n = 25) achieved sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 4.76%, 98.18%, and 48.31%; 30.95%, 87.18%, and 58.02%; and 60.0%, 100.0%, and 84.0%, respectively. PET/MRI-assessed imaging complete response showed substantial agreement with pCR (κ = 0.643). Conclusion Neoadjuvant SCRT followed by chemoimmunotherapy achieved high pCR rates in pMMR LARC. Conventional MRI and ERUS showed limited sensitivity despite relatively high specificity. 18F-FAPI PET/MRI showed potential diagnostic utility in a small subgroup, but its moderate sensitivity and limited sample size warrant further validation. These findings highlight the limitations of imaging alone and the need for comprehensive response assessment.

title: Combined radiofrequency electromagnetic and pulsed magnetic field exposure attenuates histological and molecular markers of acute colonic injury in young rats.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease involves epithelial injury, ulceration, apoptosis, inflammation, and oxidative-stress dysregulation. Although bioelectromagnetic fields may modulate tissue responses, their effects on acute colitis remain unclear. This exploratory study assessed histological and molecular changes associated with combined radiofrequency electromagnetic field (RF-EMF) and pulsed magnetic field (PMF) exposure in acetic-acid-induced colitis.Thirty-two young female Wistar albino rats were allocated to Control, Colitis, Colitis+RF-EMF+PMF, or RF-EMF+PMF groups (n=8 each). Colitis was induced intrarectally with 4% acetic acid. Exposure comprised RF-EMF (27.12 MHz, 30 min/session, 12 cycles/day) and PMF (0.5 mT, continuous). After seven days, distal colonic specimens underwent semiquantitative histopathology, crypt morphometry, immunohistochemistry for CAS-3, IL-6, and TNF-α, and RT-qPCR for SIRT-1, NRF-2, and HO-1. Colitis caused histological injury, reduced crypt dimensions, increased CAS-3, IL-6, and TNF-α immunopositivity, and decreased SIRT-1, NRF-2, and HO-1 expression. Compared with untreated colitis, combined exposure increased crypt depth and width and reduced all three immunohistochemical markers (all Tukey-adjusted p<0.001). Overall histopathological injury was lower but not statistically significant (Dunn-adjusted p=0.068), whereas submucosal inflammatory infiltration decreased significantly (p=0.048). NRF-2 expression increased (Tukey-adjusted p=0.002); SIRT-1 and HO-1 increased numerically without statistical significance (p=0.057 and 0.134).Combined RF-EMF+PMF exposure was associated with preserved crypt architecture, reduced apoptotic and inflammatory immunopositivity, and increased NRF-2 expression. Absent barrier-function testing and incomplete RF dosimetry preclude conclusions regarding restored epithelial barrier function or established therapeutic efficacy.

title: Targeting Accelerated Aging in COPD: The AMICO (A Trial of Metformin In COpd) Trial Design.
abstract: Introduction Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is increasingly recognized as a disease of accelerated biological aging characterized by progressive lung function decline, emphysema progression and multiple age-related comorbidities. Current therapies improve symptoms and reduce exacerbations but have limited effects on disease progression. Metformin has demonstrated anti-aging properties through modulation of pathways involved in oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular senescence, making it a potential disease-modifying treatment in COPD. Methods AMICO (A Trial of Metformin In COPD) is an investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial conducted in anonymous . A total of 212 patients with clinically stable COPD, centrilobular emphysema on computed tomography, post-bronchodilator FEV 1 40%-70% predicted and accelerated FEV 1 decline (>40 mL·year -1 ) will be randomized (1:1) to receive metformin (850 mg twice daily) or matching placebo for 36 months in addition to standard COPD treatment. Assessments include pulmonary function, chest computed tomography, exercise capacity, health status, muscle strength, body composition, age associated comorbidities development and aging-related biomarkers.The primary endpoint is the annual rate of FEV 1 decline over 36 months. Secondary endpoints include emphysema progression, changes in diffusing capacity, COPD Assessment Test score, 6-minute walk distance, BODE index, handgrip strength, exacerbations, major cardiovascular events, cancer incidence and renal dysfunction. Conclusions AMICO is the first randomized trial specifically designed to evaluate metformin as a gerotherapeutic and disease-modifying intervention in COPD. The study may provide novel evidence supporting geroscience-based approaches to slow disease progression and improve long-term outcomes in patients with COPD.

title: The FOXA2-BNIP3 axis alleviates acute necrotizing pancreatitis by promoting mitophagy in pancreatic acinar cells to inhibit mtDNA-mediated AIM2 inflammasome activation.
abstract: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis (ANP) is a severe inflammatory pancreatic disease characterized by pancreatic necrosis and systemic inflammation, with complex pathogenesis, rapid progression, and poor prognosis. Mitochondrial dysfunction in pancreatic acinar cells represents a pivotal early event in ANP; however, mitophagy, a central component of mitochondrial quality control, remains poorly characterized in terms of its role, regulatory networks, and therapeutic potential in ANP. In this study, we demonstrated that BNIP3 (BCL2 interacting protein 3) expression was significantly downregulated in patients with ANP and negatively correlated with inflammatory severity. Consistently, BNIP3-mediated mitophagy was impaired in the pancreatic tissue of ANP mouse models. Notably, restoration of BNIP3 expression using a novel adeno-associated virus targeting pancreatic tissue (AAV-PAN)- Bnip3 gene therapy vector alleviated pancreatic necrosis and systemic inflammatory injury, promoted mitophagy, and inhibited mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Mechanistically, BNIP3-dependent mitophagy facilitated the clearance of damaged mitochondria and prevented mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release into the cytosol, thereby suppressing AIM2 (absent in melanoma 2) inflammasome activation and subsequent acinar cell pyroptosis. Furthermore, we identified the transcription factor FOXA2 (forkhead box A2) as a direct upstream regulator that bound to the Bnip3 promoter and positively regulated its expression. FOXA2 was downregulated in ANP, whereas pancreas-specific FOXA2 overexpression activated BNIP3-mediated mitophagy and conferred protection against inflammatory injury. Together, these findings uncovered a previously unrecognized mechanism whereby the FOXA2-BNIP3-AIM2 axis mitigated pancreatic and systemic inflammatory injury in ANP by enhancing mitophagy to restrain mtDNA-dependent AIM2 inflammasome activation, highlighting the FOXA2-BNIP3-AIM2 axis as a promising target for gene therapy. title: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Salmonella Typhi spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse: a case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Spondylodiscitis is an uncommon spinal infection that remains diagnostically challenging because of its non-specific symptoms and radiological overlap with tuberculosis and neoplasms. Among these, infections caused by Salmonella Typhi are extremely unusual, and the case becomes even more challenging when multidrug resistance (MDR) is present. Presentation of case We describe a 49-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension who presented with persistent back pain following an episode of enteric fever. Imaging showed spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse, initially suspected as tuberculosis or metastasis. A mammogram and tuberculosis (TB) workup were negative. Definitive diagnosis was only achieved during surgery. Intraoperative biopsy and culture confirmed Salmonella Typhi , resistant to multiple antibiotics but sensitive to imipenem and azithromycin. Targeted therapy led to clinical improvement. Clinical discussion This case underlines the diagnostic difficulty of spinal infections, where radiology alone cannot differentiate between infection and malignancy. Surgical biopsy and culture remain essential, aligning with current Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommendations. Conclusion Multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhi spondylodiscitis is exceptionally rare. Early tissue diagnosis and tailored therapy are key to achieving favorable outcomes.
originalAbstract:
Introduction and importance

Spondylodiscitis is an uncommon spinal infection that remains diagnostically challenging because of its non-specific symptoms and radiological overlap with tuberculosis and neoplasms. Among these, infections caused by Salmonella Typhi are extremely unusual, and the case becomes even more challenging when multidrug resistance (MDR) is present.

Presentation of case

We describe a 49-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension who presented with persistent back pain following an episode of enteric fever. Imaging showed spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse, initially suspected as tuberculosis or metastasis. A mammogram and tuberculosis (TB) workup were negative. Definitive diagnosis was only achieved during surgery. Intraoperative biopsy and culture confirmed Salmonella Typhi, resistant to multiple antibiotics but sensitive to imipenem and azithromycin. Targeted therapy led to clinical improvement.

Clinical discussion

This case underlines the diagnostic difficulty of spinal infections, where radiology alone cannot differentiate between infection and malignancy. Surgical biopsy and culture remain essential, aligning with current Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommendations.

Conclusion

Multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhi spondylodiscitis is exceptionally rare. Early tissue diagnosis and tailored therapy are key to achieving favorable outcomes.

title: Progression-free survival prediction in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: where can we further improve?
abstract: Introduction Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is a biologically heterogeneous disease in which approximately one-third of patients experience primary refractoriness or relapse despite modern chemoimmunotherapy. Although clinical prognostic indices remain the cornerstone of risk stratification, they incompletely capture the biological complexity underlying disease progression. Accurate prediction of progression-free survival (PFS) is essential to support personalized treatment strategies. Areas covered This review summarizes advances in PFS prediction in DLBCL, including clinical prognostic models, quantitative PET imaging, molecular and transcriptomic classification, genomic classifiers, tumor microenvironment profiling, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based biomarkers, and integrated multimodal prognostic models. Relevant literature was identified through PubMed, with ClinicalTrials.gov searched for ongoing clinical trials; searches were updated through 3 October 2026. We discuss the strengths, limitations, and clinical applicability of these approaches. Expert opinion Future prognostic models will increasingly rely on integrated multimodal frameworks combining clinical, imaging, molecular, immune, and dynamic response biomarkers. Among these, ctDNA has emerged as one of the most promising tools for measurable residual disease assessment. However, improving patient outcomes will require moving beyond prognostic accuracy toward predictive biomarkers capable of guiding personalized treatment selection across an evolving therapeutic landscape. Prospective validation, assay standardization, and demonstration of clinical utility will be essential for translating these approaches into routine practice.

title: Epiploic appendagitis: a review of diagnosis and treatment.
abstract: Introduction Epiploic Appendigitis (EA) is a rare, self-limiting cause of acute abdominal pain, often mistaken for conditions such as appendicitis or diverticulitis due to overlapping clinical presentations. We highlight four distinct instances of EA, emphasizing its diagnostic and therapeutic nuances. Areas covered We describe primary EA successfully managed conservatively with non-steroidal anti-inflammatories. We also describe EA with concomitant intra abdominal pathology requiring surgery (i.e. appendicitis) and managed conservatively with the EA (i.e cholecystitis). We also illustrate with intraoperative and radiological imaging, the chronic sequelae of EA, a peritoneal loose body or calcified epiploic appendage. These different types of presentations underscore the role of computed tomography as the gold-standard imaging modality for diagnosing epiploic appendagitis, characterised by hallmark findings (inflamed fat-density structures, the hyper-attenuating ring sign). Expert opinion By delineating primary and secondary EA, we aim to increase awareness among clinicians to distinguish this condition from other acute abdominal pathologies. Early recognition of EA and its benign course can prevent unnecessary surgical interventions, optimising patient outcomes and reducing healthcare costs.

title: A Belgian study assessing relapsing multiple sclerosis activity through automated magnetic resonance imaging volumetry.
abstract: Aim This study assessed to what extent ico brain ms , a commercially available artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) volumetry software, detected disease activity in patients with clinically and radiologically stable relapsing multiple sclerosis (RMS), and estimated its impact on radiologists' assessments. Patients and methods We retrospectively enrolled 111 RMS patients with two consecutive MRI scans at one year interval, without relapses, progression or radiological changes while remaining on stable therapy. MRI scans were analyzed by four radiologists acting independently, and by ico brain ms . The radiologists performed their assessments both without and with ico brain ms support and categorized patient status based on lesion and brain volume changes. Results Radiologists' detection of lesion activity non-significantly increased from 6.8% to 8.6% (McNemar p = 0.215; ordinal regression p = 0.06; sign-test p = 0.08) using ico brain ms . Detection of accelerated brain volume loss increased from 2.0% to 7.7% (all p < 0.01). Inter-reader agreement improved from 36% to 56% for lesions, and from 26% to 40% for brain loss (Kendall's W, p < 0.001). Ico brain ms detected new or significantly enlarged lesions in 16.2% and accelerated brain volume loss in 6.3% of participants. Conclusion AI-assisted MRI volumetry may support radiologists to detect subclinical disease activity in patients characterized as having stable disease.

We retrospectively enrolled 111 RMS patients with two consecutive MRI scans at one year interval, without relapses, progression or radiological changes while remaining on stable therapy. MRI scans were analyzed by four radiologists acting independently, and by icobrain ms. The radiologists performed their assessments both without and with icobrain ms support and categorized patient status based on lesion and brain volume changes.

title: Instance-specific brain image registration: learning deformable fields from a single image pair without external datasets.
abstract: Objective. To eliminate the reliance on large-scale external training datasets and achieve high-precision alignment for complex brain structures by overcoming the prevalent challenges of data scarcity and domain shifts in current deep learning-based registration methods. Approach. We propose a novel Instance-Specific Deep Brain Registration Framework that independently trains a dedicated model for each specific image pair. By reconceptualizing a single image pair as an internal dataset generator, we introduce a Multi-Scale Random Patch Learning strategy to construct a diverse local-to-global sample space. Architecturally, we design a Context-Aware Flow Predictor integrated with a Recurrent Context Transfer mechanism within a coarse-to-fine paradigm. Furthermore, a Topology-Aware Adaptive Optimization strategy is incorporated during the inference phase. By dynamically tracking the local spatial folding status, it adaptively adjusts spatial regularization to effectively suppress topological distortions while maximizing voxel-level accuracy. Main results. Extensive experiments on mono-modal, multi-modal, and pathological brain MRI datasets demonstrate that our method can handle large anatomical deformations without relying on external training datasets. It achieves highly competitive registration performance compared to mainstream population-based and implicit neural representation methods. Crucially, it balances this alignment precision with effective numerical topology preservation. Significance. This framework challenges the traditional population-based learning paradigm, offering a highly flexible, robust, and promising solution for practical neuroimage analysis, particularly in clinical scenarios characterized by extreme data scarcity and complex cross-modality variations.

title: EFM-GAN: enhanced feature modeling for multimodal MRI synthesis under missing-modality settings.
abstract: Objective . Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) synthesis has been widely investigated for recovering unavailable imaging modalities under incomplete acquisition scenarios. However, existing approaches often rely on implicit feature fusion strategies, where modality-specific appearance information and cross-modal anatomical representations are entangled in a shared latent space. Such entanglement may lead to unstable feature interaction and limit the preservation of modality-invariant structural information. Moreover, although multimodal MRI sequences are generally spatially registered, modality-specific acquisition mechanisms introduce heterogeneous feature distributions, leading to feature-level semantic inconsistency during cross-modal representation learning. Lesion-related details are also frequently underrepresented, particularly in anatomically complex regions that are difficult to reconstruct. Approach . To address these limitations, an enhanced feature modeling generative adversarial network (EFM-GAN) is proposed with an explicit parallel feature modeling framework. In EFM-GAN, parallel feature branches explicitly model modality-specific appearance and cross-modal shared representations. A bidirectional progressive alignment module is further introduced to progressively reduce feature-level semantic discrepancies between modality-specific representations before feature fusion, while preserving modality-dependent appearance information. Furthermore, a reconstruction difficulty-aware loss is designed to adaptively reweight reconstruction constraints, assigning greater emphasis to regions that are harder to reconstruct. Main results . Extensive experiments on the BRaTS2020 and BRaTS2021 datasets demonstrate that EFM-GAN achieves higher peak signal-to-noise ratio and structural similarity index than the evaluated baseline methods across multiple target modalities, with improved structural consistency and synthesis fidelity. Significance . The results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly modeling modality-specific and shared representations, progressively aligning heterogeneous features, and emphasizing reconstruction-difficult regions for missing-modality MRI synthesis.

title: Volumetric chest CT report generation via state-space visual prompting and clinical-fact alignment.
abstract: Objective. To address the memory bottlenecks of three-dimensional (3D) sequence modeling and the factual hallucinations associated with cross-entropy optimization in automated 3D chest computed tomography (CT) report generation. Approach. We propose an end-to-end framework that couples perception refinement with clinical-fact alignment. First, a hybrid perception module integrates spatial visual encoding with a bidirectional state-space model to capture global anatomical topology at linear computational complexity. Second, a lesion-aware visual prompting module extracts key pathological signals through cross-view synergy and adaptive residual gating. Finally, the text decoder is fine-tuned with the group relative policy optimization algorithm under an asymmetric composite reward, reducing its reliance on normal templates. Main results. Experiments on the CTRG-Chest-548K dataset show that the proposed method achieves competitive natural language generation performance and, more importantly, a substantial improvement in clinical accuracy. The RadGraph1 score increases from 41.89 to 44.63 relative to the strongest baseline, indicating reduced factual hallucination. Significance. Combined with a 71% reduction in peak inference memory, these results indicate that the framework is a practical step toward deployable and clinically reliable automated CT interpretation.

title: 3D ultrasound shear wave elastography quantifies myocardial stiffness and anisotropy in the human heart.
abstract: Myocardial stiffness (MS) is a key property of diastolic cardiac function which is altered in various cardiomyopathies. Its quantitative evaluation remains challenging due to the myocardium's complex anisotropic fiber architecture and dynamic contraction. We developed a novel 3D shear wave elastography (3D-SWE) system suitable for clinical translation based on 3D ultrafast volumetric imaging for the quantitative assessment of myocardial stiffness in the human heart. Validation was performed on calibrated phantoms and ex vivo in porcine hearts compared to standard 2D-SWE. In vivo feasibility was demonstrated on healthy volunteers and patients with transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis. We demonstrated that 3D shear wave propagation can be observed in vivo and that 3D-SWE provides quantitative assessment of myocardium anisotropy through shear wave velocities along and across fibers and fractional anisotropy. In addition, myocardial stiffness was significantly elevated in cardiac amyloidosis patients compared to normal myocardium, whereas the fractional anisotropy was decreased. The feasibility of volumetric myocardial stiffness mapping on the human heart was demonstrated showing the potential of 3D-SWE as a clinically oriented tool for early diagnosis of cardiomyopathies such as cardiac amyloidosis.

title: 3D non-rigid motion correction using Doppler-regularized optical flow for coronary ultrasound localization microscopy in beating heart.
abstract: Objectives . Coronary microvascular disease, involving vessels smaller than 300 µ m, contributes significantly to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. However, direct visualization of coronary microcirculation remains challenging because current clinical imaging modalities lack the spatial and temporal resolution required to resolve the microvascular network. Ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) enables imaging beyond the diffraction limit and can reveal coronary microvascular structures but is altered by large motion. This work addresses 3D non-rigid motion in coronary ULM to enable more accurate reconstruction and visualization of the coronary microvascular network. Approach . Here we developed a 3D non-rigid motion correction framework based on optical flow with Doppler velocity regularization to compensate for cardiac motion in 3D ULM of beating rat hearts. Main results . The method was validated in perfused ex vivo beating rat hearts imaged with ultrafast 3D ultrasound. Motion correction enhanced microbubbles tracking density and vessels delineation, enabling visualization of microvessels below 100 µ m and velocity measurements with spatial resolution of at least 40 µ m. Significance . This framework advances volumetric assessment of coronary microcirculation, facilitating longer acquisition windows and may support future cardiovascular research and clinical applications by overcoming motion-induced limitations in 3D coronary ULM.

title: Motion-guided semi-supervised learning with dynamic kernels for cardiac cine segmentation.
abstract: Objective Accurate segmentation of full cardiac cine magnetic resonance (CMR) sequences is crucial for clinical diagnosis. Although deep learning models have become the standard for this task, they typically require exhaustive frame-by-frame supervision, making manual data annotation prohibitively time-consuming. Approach To address this, we propose a novel motion-guided semi-supervised spatiotemporal framework that propagates sparse supervision from the label of the end-diastolic (ED) frame to the entire sequence. Our framework jointly optimizes motion estimation and segmentation. First, a motion decoder estimates dense displacement fields to warp the ED label, generating high-fidelity pseudo-labels for unannotated frames. Concurrently, the segmentation network employs a Temporal Kernel Segmentation (TKS) module with dynamic convolutions to adaptively capture rapid cardiac deformations, alongside a Multi-Scale Spatial Propagator (MSP) to recover fine anatomical boundaries. The motion-derived pseudo-labels directly supervise the segmentation network, ensuring temporal coherence. Main results Extensive experiments on a multi-center cohort from three clinical centers demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms the compared methods, achieving superior segmentation accuracy and robust generalization capabilities. Significance The proposed framework effectively mitigates the burden of manual data annotation while providing temporally coherent full-cycle cardiac analysis, holding significant potential for efficient and reliable clinical assessment of cardiovascular diseases.

title: Segmentation-perturbation propagation in pretrained foundation-model embeddings versus IBSI-aligned radiomics for radiologist-assessed lung-nodule malignancy classification on the LIDC-IDRI cohort.
abstract: Objective Pretrained foundation-model (FM) embeddings are proposed as robust alternatives to handcrafted radiomic features, yet whether they better withstand segmentation-mask variability, the perturbation that radiomics intraclass-correlation (ICC) filtering exists to address, has not been tested head-to-head. We quantified how segmentation-mask perturbation propagates into feature reproducibility and downstream malignancy discrimination for FM embeddings and Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomics measured on a common cohort. Approach. Two 2D FM encoders (BiomedCLIP; RadImageNet ResNet50) were compared against IBSI-compliant radiomics (3D, 107 features; 2D, 102 features) on the full eligible Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) cohort: 556 lung nodules (300 malignant, 256 benign from radiologist consensus ratings, not pathology) from 399 patients. Up to thirteen perturbed masks per nodule (up to four reader masks, eight synthetic, one Dice-calibrated) were generated, and ICC(2,1) was computed across the ten perturbation conditions available for every nodule. Malignancy classification used L2-regularized logistic regression with patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Main results. Radiomics outperformed both foundation models on discrimination (AUC 0.940 and 0.930 for radiomics-2D/3D versus 0.833 BiomedCLIP and 0.798 RadImageNet; all radiomics-versus-FM differences significant by DeLong test, p≤10^(-7)). On perturbation stability the foundation models diverged: BiomedCLIP was statistically indistinguishable from radiomics (93.8% versus 90.2-92.5% stable features) and the most stable paradigm, whereas RadImageNet was significantly less stable (75.0%). A pre-specified diameter-stratified analysis showed the radiomics advantage narrows, and partly reverses, within size-matched strata; decision-curve analysis favoured radiomics. Significance. Two-dimensional foundation-model embeddings offered no discrimination advantage over IBSI radiomics under segmentation perturbation, and greater stability did not translate into greater accuracy. Perturbation stability is therefore decoupled from task-informativeness, and comparative benchmarks should report patient-grouped, size-stratified, calibration-aware metrics, not aggregate accuracy alone.&#xD.

A pre-specified diameter-stratified analysis showed the radiomics advantage narrows, and partly reverses, within size-matched strata; decision-curve analysis favoured radiomics. Significance. Two-dimensional foundation-model embeddings offered no discrimination advantage over IBSI radiomics under segmentation perturbation, and greater stability did not translate into greater accuracy. Perturbation stability is therefore decoupled from task-informativeness, and comparative benchmarks should report patient-grouped, size-stratified, calibration-aware metrics, not aggregate accuracy alone. .

title: Quantifying multi-lesion detection and localization in whole-body FDG PET/CT with a multimodal foundation model.
abstract: Objective . To develop a three-dimensional AI framework for detecting and localizing multiple lesions in whole-body FDG PET/CT, and to evaluate whether a pretrained PET/CT multimodal foundation model can improve lesion detection performance compared with conventional training from scratch. Approach . The AutoPET cohort comprised 1014 studies divided into 700 training, 114 validation, and 200 subject-independent test studies. Lesion masks were converted into three-dimensional bounding boxes. We developed a one-stage 3D lesion detector using a PlainConvUNet backbone to extract multi-scale encoder-decoder features for lesion classification and box regression. To leverage foundation-model representations, the PlainConvUNet backbone was initialized with weights from our previously developed multi-center PET/CT multimodal foundation model, pretrained using masked autoencoding, and subsequently fine-tuned for lesion detection. Four configurations were compared: PET+CT trained from scratch, PET only, CT only, and PET+CT initialized from the pretrained PET/CT foundation model. Detection performance was evaluated using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) and alternative FROC (AFROC) analyses, sensitivity at fixed false-positive (FP) rates, qualitative analysis, and lesion-size-stratified operating curves. Main results . Multimodal PET+CT consistently outperformed either modality alone across task-based detection metrics, demonstrating the complementary contributions of metabolic and anatomical information. Importantly, initialization from the pretrained PET/CT multimodal foundation model further enhanced lesion detection performance compared with training the same PET+CT detector from scratch, increasing absolute FROC sensitivity by 0.034-0.041 across the evaluated 1-4 FP-per-scan operating range and improving AFROC AUC by 0.028. Detection performance increased with lesion size, with small lesions remaining the most challenging. The separation between the pretrained and randomly initialized PET+CT configurations was more evident in the smaller-lesion strata, whereas their operating curves increasingly overlapped for larger lesions. Significance . This study provides a detection-centered, task-based characterization of multi-lesion analysis in whole-body PET/CT. Multimodal PET+CT improves lesion detection compared with either modality alone, lesion size is a major determinant of detection performance, and initialization from a pretrained PET/CT multimodal foundation model provides an additional performance improvement without modifying the downstream detector architecture.

title: Experimental Validation of Skull Acoustic Modelling Strategies for Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Simulation: A Cross-Comparison Study.
abstract: Objective Accurate acoustic modelling of the skull is important for simulation-guided transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) applications. However, existing skull parameterization strategies vary widely in complexity and reported accuracy. This study systematically evaluates commonly used modelling approaches to determine their predictive performance across multiple frequencies and skull types. Approach Five skull modelling strategies were assessed: two voxel-wise linear mapping models, one with fixed attenuation coefficient and one with Hounsfield unit (HU)-dependent attenuation coefficients; two three-layer models with fixed and skull-density ratio (SDR) dependent attenuation coefficient; and one single-layer fixed-parameter model. Nineteen regions of interest from five historical and two Thiel-embalmed human skulls were examined at 220 kHz, 680 kHz and 1000 kHz, bowl-surface source fields were reconstructed using holography, and intracranial pressure distributions were captured with a needle hydrophone. Measurements were compared with k-Wave simulations. Results Average simulated peak pressure errors (ɛp) ranged from 20% to 31% across frequencies, whereas intensity errors (ɛI) reached 41% to 81%. Errors in -6 dB focal volume ranged from 18% to 65%, and focal position discrepancies were typically several millimeters. Simulation generally predicted smaller insertion losses than measured, indicating a tendency to underestimate skull-related attenuation and overestimate transmitted intracranial exposure. Among the five modelling strategies, the model with the lowest observed error varied with frequency and outcome. Paired specimen-level comparisons did not establish a consistent accuracy advantage for any strategy. Significance These results indicate that current skull modelling strategies may reproduce the gross intracranial beam pattern while still misestimating the delivered acoustic exposure, focal coverage and localization. Such errors are directly relevant to tFUS dose selection, target coverage and safety-margin interpretation, underscoring the need for refined parameterization methods for reliable tFUS treatment planning.&#xD.

title: Artificial intelligence for cerebrovascular digital subtraction angiography: methods, evidence, and challenges.
abstract: Cerebrovascular diseases remain a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) provides high-spatiotemporal-resolution visualization of cerebrovascular anatomy and contrast-agent dynamics and plays an important role in diagnosis, interventional treatment planning, and treatment assessment. Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied to cerebrovascular DSA, yet the available evidence is distributed across diverse imaging settings, technical tasks, datasets, and validation strategies. This structured topical review provides a DSA-centered overview of AI-assisted cerebrovascular image analysis across 2D DSA, three-dimensional rotational angiography, and four-dimensional DSA. Literature from Web of Science Core Collection and major engineering databases was screened at title, abstract, and full-text levels using predefined eligibility criteria. The literature is organized around six interconnected tasks: image preprocessing, vessel and lesion segmentation, image registration, reconstruction and generation, disease diagnosis and detection, and hemodynamic analysis. Representative conventional and learning-based methods are reviewed together with their datasets, evaluation metrics, validation designs, and available data or code resources, with particular attention to the strength and limitations of the supporting evidence. Recent studies demonstrate increasing use of spatiotemporal modeling, deep learning, and image-generation techniques, but clinical translation remains constrained by small or single-center datasets, heterogeneous acquisition protocols and evaluation practices, limited external and prospective validation, model interpretability, and deployment requirements. Future work should emphasize acquisition-aware and physics-informed modeling, multicenter and privacy-preserving collaboration, clinically meaningful validation, and closer integration with neurointerventional workflows. By linking methodological developments with their supporting evidence and translational challenges, this review aims to support the development of more robust and clinically applicable AI methods for cerebrovascular DSA.

title: SPARC: Sectorized Partial-Angle Reconstruction Based Motion Correction Method for Multi-Phase CCTA.
abstract: Objective Multi-phase Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography (CCTA) provides a clear visualization of coronary arteries, offering comprehensive and reliable imaging support for the clinical diagnosis of coronary artery disease. However, traditional motion correction reconstruction algorithms lack reconstruction robustness despite their interpretability, while deep learning reconstruction methods achieve high imaging quality at the expense of interpretability and anatomical reliability in clinical CCTA practice. This study aims to simultaneously achieve interpretable and robust multi-phase coronary reconstruction. Approach. We propose a motion trajectory estimation and motion correction framework termed sectorized partial-angle reconstruction-based motion correction (SPARC) for CCTA. The proposed framework integrates sectorized partial-angle reconstructions, a spatio-temporal cascaded network for coronary centerline extraction, and a phase-accumulated fuzzy C-means clustering algorithm for motion trajectory estimation. These components work together to minimize motion estimation errors and enhance the quality of motion-corrected reconstruction. Main results. Experimental results from both simulations and clinical studies demonstrate that SPARC achieves superior reconstruction performance compared with existing methods. SPARC effectively reduces coronary motion artifacts and restores clear vessel structures while preserving reconstruction fidelity, achieving the best scores on all metrics. Significance. By preserving both interpretability and anatomical reliability while effectively reducing motion artifacts, SPARC provides a clinically deployable solution for motion-corrected multi-phase CCTA, supporting more reliable imaging for coronary artery disease diagnosis.

title: Sampling-free Monte Carlo dropout approximation for single-pass uncertainty quantification in deep learning-based PET reconstructions.
abstract: Objective Medical image reconstructions using deep learning (DL) can rapidly generate high-quality images from degraded measurements, but their clinical adoption remains challenging, largely due to the lack of fast and reliable methods to quantify aleatoric (data-driven) and epistemic (model-driven) uncertainties on a per-prediction basis. We aim to develop a computationally efficient approach for estimating both uncertainties at the voxel level in DL-based image reconstruction within a single inference run. Approach: We present a moment propagation-based framework that analytically approximates the conventional, multi-realization Monte Carlo (MC) dropout by propagating feature-map means and marginal variances through network layers, followed by a pre-calibrated correction table to compensate for covariance effects omitted in the approximation. This enables joint estimation of reconstruction, aleatoric uncertainty and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. The proposed framework was implemented on top of FastPET -- a network model synthesizing PET reconstructions from time-of-flight histo-images -- and evaluated in a patient pilot study of 26 total-body PET/CT acquisitions (16 [18F]-FDG and 10 [18F]-PSMA cases). Main Results: Proposed method achieved relatively strong agreement with the 50-pass MC approach, with absolute differences <0.5% for reconstruction, <4.2% for aleatoric uncertainty and <9.8% for epistemic uncertainty, along with narrow spreads across patients and tracer types, while reducing computation time by ~40-fold. In a complementary proof-of-concept low-count experiment, regional tracer uptake confidence intervals (CIs, derived from propagated uncertainties) widened with increased noise level, and reference uptakes consistently fell close to CI boundaries, indicating the proposed method could provide roughly calibrated uncertainty magnitudes reflecting quantitative prediction errors. Significance: The proposed approach provides a sampling-free and relatively accurate approximation to the multi-pass MC-based uncertainty estimation in the histo-image-based DL PET reconstruction framework. Per-prediction uncertainty quantification enables direct assessment of AI confidence and potentially supports more reliable and informed decision-making.

title: Closed-form, engine-portable uncertainty prediction of deformable image registration for dose accumulation in adaptive radiotherapy.
abstract: Objective Voxel-level uncertainty estimates of the deformation vector field (DVF) produced by commercial deformable image registration (DIR) engines are flagged as an open issue by AAPM TG-132 but seldom available, preventing principled propagation into accumulated dose-volume histograms (DVHs). We propose and validate an engine-portable per-voxel σ predictor for the DVF (μ) of a deterministic DIR, calibrated by one scalar f against landmark Target Registration Error (TRE), with no access to the engine's internals. Approach. The framework combines (i) an anisotropic Gaussian correlation kernel, longer along the cranio-caudal axis, generalising the isotropic kernel of Smolders et al. (2023); and (ii) a heuristic-residual σ_h=f[wR̃+(1-w)d̃] (default w=0.7), where R̃ combines a self-similarity descriptor residual with an image-gradient suppression factor and d̃ is |Jacobian determinant-1|, both normalised to [0,1]; σ_h is closed-form, computed from the image pair and the DVF without optimisation or training. For each combination of dataset and DIR engine (a cell), f is calibrated against TRE via grid search minimising the Landmark Expected Calibration Error (LECE). Main results. Across 4 publicly annotated computed tomography datasets (Lung-, Abdominal- and Liver-DIR-QA and DIR-LAB Castillo; 44,778 landmarks) and 4 DIR engines (ANTs SyNRA, ConvexAdam, uniGradICON, Elastix), with f fitted on other patients (5-fold cross-validation), the calibrated σ_h achieves, in the per-direction convention of Smolders et al., LECE within or below their 0.41-1.34mm range in all 16 cells (cases with final root-mean-square TRE ≤10mm retained). A constant σ calibrated likewise also meets this range, but the variation of σ_h raises the held-out log-likelihood in 13 cells; σ_h ranks landmarks by error only weakly (Spearman ρ=-0.11 to +0.34). Significance. A one-scalar, post-hoc calibration yields voxel-level DVF uncertainty for any deterministic DIR that exports its DVF, partly addressing the AAPM TG-132 gap; propagation into accumulated DVH bands is illustrated on one lung stereotactic body radiotherapy case.

title: Noninvasive pulse wave velocity measurement: technological progress, clinical validation, and translation challenges.
abstract: Pulse wave velocity (PWV) is increasingly recognized as a vital noninvasive metric for assessing arterial stiffness and an established independent predictor of cardiovascular risk. Despite its well-recognized clinical value, the accurate and reliable measurement of PWV remains methodologically challenging due to inherent physical ambiguities, technological heterogeneity across devices, and a lack of comparability between measurements obtained by different systems. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the physical foundations, mainstream detection technologies, signal-processing pipelines, and current clinical standardization status for PWV assessment. Although classical frameworks such as the Moens-Korteweg and Bramwell-Hill equations theoretically link PWV to the mechanical properties of the arterial wall, the intrinsic dependence of PWV on instantaneous blood pressure complicates the precise evaluation of structural arterial stiffness in clinical settings. We categorize existing measurement modalities into four principal types: mechanical-pressure sensing, optical techniques, advanced medical imaging, and emerging contactless approaches, each demonstrating unique trade-offs among measurement fidelity, clinical applicability, and operational convenience. Presently, three major barriers hinder the clinical translation of novel technologies: insufficient operational automation, inadequate cross-population validation, and a scarcity of longitudinal prognostic evidence. Future transformative advancements will likely rely on AI-driven, fully automated continuous monitoring systems optimized for real-world daily settings, large-scale multicenter trials across diverse demographics, and extensive long-term cohort studies utilizing wearable devices. These developments will collectively extend PWV assessment from intermittent clinical evaluation toward decentralized, personalized cardiovascular risk management.

title: Multivariate Searchlight Decoding of Structural Disconnection and Network Features for Predicting Post-Stroke Deficits.
abstract: Objective Lesion-symptom mapping and structural disconnection analyses have advanced our understanding of post-stroke deficits but remain predominantly based on forward inference, limiting identification of regions specifically predictive of behavioral impairment. We developed a multivariate voxelwise searchlight decoding framework for inverse inference integrating probabilistic structural disconnection with network-topological features. Approach. The analysis included 326 stroke patients from the GRECogVASC cohort assessed six months after stroke. For each patient, an age-specific probabilistic structural disconnection map was reconstructed using normative diffusion MRI tractography from 403 healthy controls. Within each voxel-centered searchlight, four features were extracted: disconnection probability, degree, clustering coefficient, and closeness centrality. Support vector machine classifiers were trained within deficit-specific decoding spaces using balanced bootstrap aggregation and majority voting to predict motor, executive, and processing-action-speed impairments. Statistical significance was assessed using 1,000 permutations, retaining voxels that consistently performed above chance across bootstrap iterations. Decoding-derived regions were subsequently assessed for within-cohort individual-level classification. Main results. Initial validation focused on left and right motor impairments, identifying predictive regions primarily within the contralateral precentral gyrus, internal capsule, and corticospinal tract, with mean accuracy ranges of 68.7-77.9%, 66.4-74.6%, and 64.8-71.8%, respectively. At the individual level, decoding-derived masks preserved overall classification performance, with accuracy improvements of up to 2.6% for individual deficits while reducing voxel dimensionality by up to 95.4%. Executive dysfunction and processing-action-speed deficits showed statistically above-chance but lower accuracies (54.5-66.9%). Executive dysfunction involved predominantly left-lateralized frontotemporal regions, whereas processing-action-speed deficits involved distributed fronto-insular, temporal, parietal, visual-association, and commissural pathways. Significance. The multivariate searchlight decoding framework integrating structural disconnection and network topology provides an inverse-inference approach complementary to lesion- and disconnection-symptom mapping for identifying spatially specific predictive patterns after stroke. The strong motor findings provide proof-of-concept support for the approach, whereas the cognitive results support its extension to distributed behavioral domains while underscoring the need for independent replication before neuroanatomical or clinical interpretation (Clinical trial registration: NCT01339195).

title: FASA-Net: A Frequency-Domain-Enhanced and Anatomically Constrained Vision-Language Framework for Automated Chest X-ray Report Generation.
abstract: Automated radiology report generation can reduce radiologists' workloads by producing preliminary reports from medical images. However, generating chest X-ray reports remains challenging. Subtle lesions and organ boundaries may be underrepresented, visual regions may be poorly aligned with medical terminology, and long reports require coherent clinical descriptions. To address these challenges, we propose FASA-Net, a vision-language framework that combines frequency-domain enhancement with anatomical semantic constraints. Its Frequency-Domain Pyramid Attention Network (FPAN) integrates frequency-domain analysis and a multiscale feature pyramid to enhance local structures and high-frequency visual details. The Anatomical Semantic Constraint Attention (ASCA) module guides cross-modal interactions between visual regions and anatomy-related terms to reduce the risk of regional misalignment and semantic hallucination. The Context Aggregation Module (CAM) incorporates a summary of the text generated so far into decoding to improve coherence and terminological consistency. Experiments on the public IU X-Ray and MIMIC-CXR datasets show competitive performance on natural language generation metrics, including BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE-L, together with improved clinical label consistency measured using CheXbert-based clinical efficacy metrics. Ablation studies, visualizations, and case studies further illustrate the contributions of FPAN, ASCA, and CAM to visual detail enhancement, anatomical semantic alignment, and contextual aggregation. FASA-Net therefore has potential as an auxiliary tool for chest X-ray report generation, although clinical deployment requires further validation using multicenter data, radiologist assessments, and prospective studies.

title: Stable training and confidence‑calibrated generation of urinary stone CT images via physics‑constrained GANs under small‑sample conditions.
abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence has become integral to modern medicine. Deep learning algorithms are widely used to assist clinical diagnosis, and medical image synthesis has become increasingly mature. However, in small-sample scenarios, synthetic images often overlook infrequent but clinically valuable lesion features. To address the challenges of training instability, insufficient authenticity, and limited clinical usability, we propose a two-stage framework based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). In the first stage, we establish a stable training and physical prior constraint framework for small-sample CT images. Specifically, we incorporate an established asymmetric normalization strategy into the WGAN-GP framework to balance generator convergence and the discriminator's Lipschitz constraint, and we embed a physical noise simulation layer at the discriminator's front end, combined with partial volume effect gradient regularization, to enhance the realism of synthesized images. In the second stage, we employ MC Dropout and deep ensemble methods to quantify uncertainty, generating uncertainty heatmaps and physically consistent confidence maps based on the Poisson-Gaussian noise model. This assists physicians in locating abnormal areas and reducing misdiagnosis risks. Through joint optimization of the generation framework, uncertainty quantification, and confidence image output, the proposed framework effectively resolves issues of mode collapse, low confidence, and poor clinical usability under small-sample conditions. The proposed framework achieves a competitive FID of 128.0, an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.072, and a high-risk recall rate of 88% for stone boundary regions, demonstrating its potential for clinically reliable synthetic CT generation.

title: Mitigating over-smoothing in Mamba via high-frequency-guided feature optimization for medical image segmentation.
abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in medical image segmentation owing to their efficient global context modeling capabilities. However, the sequential scanning mechanism of SSMs tends to induce feature over-smoothing, attenuating high-frequency lesion details and blurring irregular boundaries. In this paper, we propose HFG-Mamba, a Vision Mamba network architecture driven by high-frequency-guided feature optimization. With marginal computational and parameter overhead, the proposed architecture achieves a synergy between high-frequency prior extraction and boundarysemantic interaction. Specifically, a high-frequency prior guidance branch built upon the Discrete Wavelet Transform provides the backbone with high-frequency spatial priors. The Spatial Recalibration Fusion Block leverages these priors to counteract over-smoothing by recalibrating backbone features. The decoder further incorporates a Boundary-Semantic Interaction Module to restore boundary details degraded during upsampling. Moreover, a structure-preserving deep supervision strategy is introduced to address the optimization difficulties arising from gradient vanishing and boundary sparsity. Experiments on the ISIC17, ISIC18, and Kvasir-SEG datasets indicate that HFG-Mamba exhibits competitive performance, effectively delineating irregular boundaries and suppressing background artifacts.

title: CMRCUNet: a cross-modal calibration U-Net for acute ischaemic stroke lesion segmentation from multi-sequence MRI.
abstract: Purpose Acute ischaemic stroke is a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, and rapid delineation of infarct lesions on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is important for supporting time-sensitive treatment decisions. Multi-sequence MRI, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), provides complementary information for characterising acute ischaemic lesions. However, many deep learning approaches process these modalities using shared encoders and direct skip connections, which may limit modality-specific feature learning and remain challenged by the severe foreground-background imbalance characteristic of stroke lesion segmentation. Method: We propose CMRCUNet, a multimodal segmentation framework that combines modality-specific residual encoders, a Cross-Modal Calibration (CMC) module, and an attention-gated decoder. The modality-specific encoders independently learn sequence-dependent representations from DWI, ADC, and FLAIR, while the CMC module performs adaptive, input-dependent weighting of modality-specific features at multiple resolution levels before decoder fusion. Focal Tversky Loss is used to address severe lesion-background imbalance. The framework is evaluated in both 2D and 2.5D configurations; the 2.5D configuration incorporates neighbouring axial slices to provide limited through-plane contextual information while retaining two-dimensional convolutional operations. Test-time augmentation (TTA) is additionally evaluated to improve inference robustness. Results: CMRCUNet was evaluated on the ISLES 2022 dataset using a patient-level evaluation protocol with an independent 37-patient test cohort. The 2.5D configuration combined with TTA achieved a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.792 ± 0.142, sensitivity of 0.854 ± 0.132, specificity of 0.996 ± 0.012, and a 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 8.21 ± 8.70 mm. Conclusion: CMRCUNet provides a multimodal framework that integrates modality-specific feature extraction, adaptive cross-modal calibration, attention-gated decoding, and limited inter-slice contextual information for acute ischaemic stroke lesion segmentation. The results support further investigation of adaptive cross-modal calibration, particularly through external multi-centre validation.

title: Optimizing Rib Remodeling: A Data-Driven Model for Personalized Waist Contouring.
abstract: Background Rib cage remodeling procedures, like rib osteotomy with osteosynthesis, have shown promise for waist narrowing in aesthetic surgery. However, the ideal osteotomy location and bending angle remain poorly defined. Objectives This preclinical, proof-of-concept study aimed to: (1) quantify how osteotomy location and rib bending angle affect rib apex displacement using a large, computed tomography (CT) dataset, and (2) develop a data-driven framework as a first step toward guiding selection of rib number, osteotomy site, and bending angle tailored to individual waist contour goals. Methods Using the open-source RibFrac CT dataset, 600 ribs (300 eleventh [XI] and 300 tenth [X]) were segmented with the RibSeg deep learning tool. A custom MATLAB script simulated 15 bending scenarios per rib by varying osteotomy location (7 cm, 8 cm, 9 cm from midline) and bending angles (10°, 20°, 30°, 45°, 55°). Displacement at the rib apex was computed using a chord-perpendicular method. A graphical user interface (GUI) allowed for manual interaction, and a linear mixed-effects model quantified the effects of angle, osteotomy location, and their interaction. Results Both bending angle and osteotomy distance significantly affected apex displacement (p < 0.001), with a negative interaction indicating reduced effect of angle at more lateral osteotomy points. Rib X showed greater displacement overall than rib XI. Conclusions This proof-of-concept model establishes a biomechanical foundation for individualized rib remodeling planning. While prospective clinical validation is needed, the framework is adaptable to patient-specific imaging across age, sex, and BMI, and may ultimately support personalized surgical decision-making.

title: A multi-reader multi-case study comparing Breast Cancer Reading Efficiency and Accuracy in Screening with Tomosynthesis versus AI-assisted mammography.
abstract: Objectives Full-field digital mammography (FFDM) is the standard for breast cancer screening but has reduced sensitivity in dense breasts. Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) improves cancer detection compared to 2D mammography but is limited by cost and longer reading times. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced mammography has demonstrated improved sensitivity compared to 2D mammography. This study compares AI-enhanced 2D mammography (DM+AI) with DBT in recalling interval breast cancers (IBCs). Methods : A multi-reader, multi-case crossover study was conducted using the Emory BrEast Imaging Dataset, which includes paired FFDM and DBT images with biopsy-proven outcomes. Six radiologists reviewed 53 IBC and 53 screen-detected cancer (SDC) cases, with random assignment to DM+AI or DBT, followed by crossover after a washout period. Primary outcomes included recall rate of IBCs. Secondary outcomes included recall rate of SDCs, interpretation time, and subgroup analysis by breast density. Results : For IBCs, DM+AI and DBT demonstrated similar recall rates (41.5% vs 40.9%) and detection rates (14.8% vs 11.9%). DM+AI identified more non-invasive (31.5% vs 13.0%) and mass-forming (61.0% vs 21.8%) cancers. For SDCs, recall and detection rates were comparable across modalities. In fatty breasts, recall was higher with DM+AI (91.7% vs 50.0%), while DBT performed better in extremely dense breasts. DM+AI enabled faster interpretation, averaging 24.1 seconds less per case. Conclusion : AI-enhanced 2D mammography demonstrated comparable performance to DBT with shorter interpretation times, supporting a stratified screening approach. Advances in knowledge This study is the first direct comparison of AI-enhanced mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis for IBC detection.

title: Quantitative Hepatobiliary MRI for Early Prognostic Assessment After Liver Transplantation: Survival Prediction Using the Contrast Enhancement Index.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the feasibility and prognostic value of the contrast enhancement index (CEI) derived from gadobenate dimeglumine (Gd-BOPTA)-enhanced hepatobiliary-phase (HBP) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for early assessment of liver graft function after liver transplantation (LT). Methods This retrospective study included LT recipients undergoing Gd-BOPTA-enhanced MRI within 6 months after transplantation. CEI was calculated using liver-to-psoas signal intensity ratios on pre-contrast and HBP images acquired 90-120 minutes after contrast administration. ROC, Kaplan-Meier, and age-adjusted Cox regression analyses evaluated associations with mortality. Results Seventy patients (median age, 62 years; interquartile range [IQR], 48-74) were included. title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Procedural Efficiency of ACR TI-RADS, EU-TIRADS, and K-TIRADS in ≤ 10 mm Thyroid Nodules Using Bethesda Cytology: A Cohort of 998 Nodules.
abstract: Objectives To compare the diagnostic performance and procedural efficiency of American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (ACR TI-RADS), European Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (EU-TIRADS), and Korean Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (K-TIRADS) in ≤ 10 mm nodules using Bethesda cytology as the reference standard. Methods This retrospective study included 998 nodules ≤10 mm undergoing ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB). Primary analyses included Bethesda II (negative) and Bethesda V-VI (positive) nodules excluding Bethesda I/III/IV, yielding 604 nodules (540 negative; 64 positive). Categories 1-3 were considered low risk and 4-5 high risk under a harmonized threshold Diagnostic performance and classification patterns were compared. Results K-TIRADS showed the numerically highest sensitivity (93.8%) and negative predictive value (NPV) (97.9%), although sensitivity did not differ significantly between systems, with lower specificity (35.4%) and accuracy (41.6%).EU-TIRADS showed intermediate performans (sensitivity 68.8%, specificity 73.7%, accuracy 73.2%). ACR TI-RADS achieved the highest specificity (83.3%) and accuracy (81.0%) with lower sensitivity (60.9%). Low-risk classification rates were 78.6% (ACR), 69.2% (EU), and 32.3% (K) of nodules; false-positive high-risk classifications among Bethesda II nodules were 16.7%, 26.3%, and 64.6%, respectively. Conclusion In ≤ 10 mm nodules, the three systems demonstrated distinct diagnostic and classification profiles under a harmonized TR4-5 threshold, with different trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity. Advances in knowledge Applying a harmonized TR4-5 threshold in ≤ 10 mm nodules reveals substantially differences in classification patterns among the three systems, demonstrating that they are not interchangeable under a uniform risk threshold.

title: Construction and Validation of a Prediction Model for TACE Resistance in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Based on Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Radiomics.
abstract: Objective To construct and validate a contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) radiomics-clinical model for predicting transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods A total of 168 HCC patients who underwent CEUS on two vendor platforms (Philips E9 and GE Logiq E95) were split into a training set (n = 118) and an internal validation set (n = 50), with an additional 80 patients forming an external validation cohort. For each patient, 2D regions of interest were manually delineated on the largest cross-sectional slice of each CEUS phase. Radiomic features were extracted and screened by LASSO regression; the twelve retained features were linearly combined into a single Rad-score. The Rad-score and three prespecified clinical risk factors (tumor size, Child-Pugh class, AFP) confirmed by multivariate analysis were combined into a parsimonious logistic regression (LR) model with four predictors in total. Performance was assessed by ROC curve, calibration curve, decision curve analysis (DCA), subgroup analysis, and prospective validation. Results The combined model had AUCs of 0.895, 0.891 and 0.846 in three sets, with subgroup AUCs >0.86. Prospective validation showed TACE plus sorafenib improved 6-month response rate from 26.7% to 53.3% for high-risk patients. Conclusion The CEUS radiomics-clinical model accurately predicts TACE resistance, guiding individualized HCC treatment. Advances in knowledge This model integrates CEUS multi-phase radiomics and clinical factors, outperforming single clinical/radiomic models. Strict multi-step screening and comprehensive validation avoid data leakage, ensuring robust prediction and clinical translatability.

title: Seeing the Gaps: Heatmaps, Metrics, and the Hidden Failures of Explainable AI in Dentomaxillofacial Radiology - A Systematic Review.
abstract: Objectives This systematic review aims to evaluate the techniques and reported patterns of heatmap-based visual explanations in deep learning (DL) systems for dental radiographic classification tasks. Methods A literature search following PRISMA guidelines was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore Library, Oria.no and Google Scholar to retrieve studies using DL for dental classification tasks. Only articles with a visual explanation (heatmap) were selected. Risk of bias assessment was done with QUADAS-2, PROBAST-AI and CEBM. The heatmap technique, reasons for inclusion, explanations provided and patterns were analysed. Results In the 136 studies reviewed, Grad-CAM was the most commonly used technique. The predominant reason for using visual explanations was to understand the decision-making process of the DL model. Some heatmaps reflect established radiographic criteria, while others exhibit unique, label-dependent patterns that sometimes emphasise irrelevant areas. Cropping to the region of interest influences visual explanations. Conclusions Visual explanations seem clinically plausible to domain experts when aligned with domain knowledge, but clinical plausibility does not equal technical faithfulness. Formal faithfulness testing was rarely performed among the included studies. Therefore, explanations should not be assumed to accurately represent the model's underlying reasoning. Limitations include the evaluation of studies not primarily designed for visual explanation assessment. No funding was received for this review. Authors declare no competing interests. Advances in knowledge Visual explanations, while clinically plausible when aligned with domain knowledge, remain insufficiently validated and should not be assumed to faithfully represent model reasoning. An implausible explanation does not necessarily indicate model failure. Domain/task-specific evaluation metrics for explainable AI in dentomaxillofacial radiology are needed.

title: Enhancing Cone-Beam Computed Tomography Image Quality Using Deep Learning-based Super-Resolution.
abstract: Objectives To develop deep learning super-resolution (SR) models for enhancing cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). Methods Seventy CBCT volumes (75 µm voxel size) served as references. Paired low-resolution (LR) volumes (300 µm) were simulated using physics-based degradation. Four architectures were each trained with three loss configurations (L1; L1+edge; L1+edge+perceptual): Swin Transformer for Image Restoration (SwinIR), Hybrid Attention Transformer (HAT), Hybrid Multi-Axis Aggregation Network (HMA-Net), and Dense-Residual-Connected Transformer (DRCT). Performance was assessed with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index measure (SSIM), learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), and deep image structure and texture similarity (DISTS). Three dentists ranked the 12 configurations in 28 sets using blinded forced-choice pairwise comparisons. Correlations of metrics and expert ranks were assessed using Spearman correlation. Results All configurations outperformed LR input and bicubic interpolation on every metric (p < 0.05). HMA-Net trained with L1+edge+perceptual loss performed best on LPIPS (0.216) and DISTS (0.186). HAT with L1 loss achieved the highest PSNR (28.79 dB) and SSIM (0.820). Experts ranked DRCT and HAT with L1 loss, and DRCT with L1+edge loss, as the best configurations (p < 0.001 versus others). Expert rank correlated moderately only with PSNR (rho = -0.65) and SSIM (rho = -0.60; both p < 0.05). Conclusions Transformer-based SR improved the perceived quality of clinical CBCT images. HAT and DRCT trained with L1 pixel loss alone, and DRCT trained with L1 and edge loss, demonstrated superior performance. Advances in knowledge Transformer-based super-resolution improved expert-perceived detail of simulated low-resolution in vivo CBCT scans without additional radiation dose, supporting further validation on directly acquired low-resolution scans.

title: Lessons learned from a decade of EUS(-FNA) staging in esophageal and GEJ carcinoma: towards a selective staging strategy.
abstract: Endoscopic ultrasonography with fine-needle aspiration (EUS(-FNA)) is recommended by current guidelines as part of the staging for esophageal and gastro-esophageal junction (GEJ) carcinoma, yet its incremental value over modern 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) remains uncertain. This Lessons Learned article reflects on over a decade of EUS(-FNA) and FDG-PET staging in 402 patients with potentially curable esophageal or GEJ carcinoma at a high-volume tertiary referral center. In 91.3% of patients, EUS(-FNA) did not alter the radiation field as would have been defined by FDG-PET. EUS(-FNA) resulted in an expansion of the radiation field in 4.5% and reduction in 4.2% of patients. Squamous cell carcinoma showed more than two-fold greater likelihood of radiation field modification. Among 193 patients classified as FDG-PET non-suspicious for malignant lymph nodes (LNs), EUS-FNA identified malignant LNs in eight patients (4.1%), which influenced the radiation field. In 5 of 402 patients (1.2%) a malignant LN was detected with EUS-FNA in a station that would not have routinely been resected surgically. In patients planned for neoadjuvant or definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT), LN staging is of direct therapeutic consequence: underestimation of nodal disease may result in geographic miss, while overestimation leads to unnecessary irradiation. In contrast, in patients treated with perioperative 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin and docetaxel (FLOT) followed by surgical lymphadenectomy, most involved LN stations are routinely addressed surgically, limiting the added value of EUS(-FNA) for treatment planning. Therefore, we view EUS(-FNA) as a selective staging tool in patients planned for neoadjuvant or definitive CRT, rather than a procedure applied routinely to all patients.

title: Liver radiomics on routine cardiac CT identifies hepatic stress states that predict heart failure.
abstract: Aims Heart failure (HF) prevention remains limited because early multisystem cardiometabolic dysfunction is not captured by conventional risk tools. We evaluated whether liver radiomic phenotypes derived opportunistically from coronary artery calcium computed tomography (CAC-CT) identify imaging-defined hepatic stress states associated with incident HF. Methods and results We analysed 59 237 individuals undergoing CAC-CT (CLARIFY: 46 028; Houston Methodist: 13 209). Liver regions were segmented and radiomic features extracted to derive a Liver Radiomics Score (LRS). The model was trained in a CLARIFY derivation cohort (Dtr, n = 9205), validated in a hold-out cohort (Dts, n = 36 823), and externally evaluated in Houston Methodist (Dext, n = 13 209). The mean follow-up was 1411 days (SD 760.1) in the pooled Dtr and Dts cohorts (1144 HF events) and 470 days (SD 596) in Dext (212 HF events). Continuous LRS was associated with incident HF [Dts: hazard ratio (HR) 1.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.52-1.74; P < 0.001; Dext: HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.07; P = 0.004] and remained significant after multivariable adjustment in Dts. Increasing LRS quartiles showed progressively adverse hepatic, haemodynamic, and cardiometabolic profiles and higher HF risk. Among 17 806 Dts participants with PREVENT data, adding LRS modestly improved discrimination across CAC- and PREVENT-based models (P < 0.001) and improved reclassification metrics (7-year net reclassification improvement up to 0.25; including integrated discrimination improvement up to 0.015). High LRS identified elevated risk in low-risk groups: among participants with CAC=0, high LRS conferred ∼2.5-fold higher 5-year HF incidence, and ∼2.9-fold in PREVENT-low individuals. Conclusion In this large multicentre cohort, liver radiomics from CAC-CT captured hepatic stress states linked to HF risk and modestly improved risk stratification beyond CAC and PREVENT scores.

Heart failure (HF) prevention remains limited because early multisystem cardiometabolic dysfunction is not captured by conventional risk tools. We evaluated whether liver radiomic phenotypes derived opportunistically from coronary artery calcium computed tomography (CAC-CT) identify imaging-defined hepatic stress states associated with incident HF.

Methods and results

We analysed 59 237 individuals undergoing CAC-CT (CLARIFY: 46 028; Houston Methodist: 13 209). Liver regions were segmented and radiomic features extracted to derive a Liver Radiomics Score (LRS). The model was trained in a CLARIFY derivation cohort (Dtr, n = 9205), validated in a hold-out cohort (Dts, n = 36 823), and externally evaluated in Houston Methodist (Dext, n = 13 209). The mean follow-up was 1411 days (SD 760.1) in the pooled Dtr and Dts cohorts (1144 HF events) and 470 days (SD 596) in Dext (212 HF events). In this large multicentre cohort, liver radiomics from CAC-CT captured hepatic stress states linked to HF risk and modestly improved risk stratification beyond CAC and PREVENT scores.

title: Long-term Prognostic Value of Sequential Coronary CT Angiography and Quantitative PET in Suspected Chronic Coronary Syndromes: A Multicentre study.
abstract: Background and aims The long-term prognostic value of a guideline-recommended selective sequential anatomical-functional imaging strategy using coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) followed by quantitative [15O]H2O positron emission tomography (PET) remains uncertain. We evaluated its long-term prognostic value in patients with first symptoms suggestive of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). Methods In this multicentre European cohort, symptomatic patients first underwent CCTA and were selectively referred to quantitative [15O]H2O PET in case of suspected obstructive stenosis (≥50%). Patients were stratified according to CCTA findings and PET-derived ischaemia (normal CCTA; non-obstructive CAD on CCTA; obstructive CAD on CCTA without ischaemia; obstructive CAD on CCTA with ischaemia). The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), and hospitalization for unstable angina (UA). Adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) were calculated. Results Among 3,918 patients (61.0±9.8 years; 54.3% female) with a median follow-up of 5.1 [3.8-8.0] years, 278 (7.1%) experienced the primary endpoint. aHRs increased stepwise across CCTA-PET categories. Compared to normal CCTA, non-obstructive CAD and obstructive CAD without ischaemia were associated with a higher risk of the combined primary endpoint (aHR 1.89, [95%CI: 1.23-2.91], p=0.004; aHR 3.20, [95%CI: 1.95-5.25], p<0.001). Among patients with obstructive CAD on CCTA, PET-derived ischaemia further increased the risk of the primary endpoint (aHR 1.55, [95%CI: 1.05-2.30]; p=0.029), but not when excluding UA from the composite endpoint (aHR 1.37, [95%CI 0.90-2.07]; p=0.141). PET-derived ischaemia primarily predicted events within the first year, while obstructive CCTA findings remained associated with long-term hard outcomes. Conclusions A sequential strategy combining CCTA and quantitative [15O]H2O PET provides robust and incremental long-term risk stratification. While PET-derived ischaemia refines prediction of short-term and symptom-driven events, CCTA-derived CAD remains the principal determinant of long-term hard outcomes.
